chapters.summary: Council staff asks attendees to settle down, silence electronics, and explains how to testify. They instruct the public not to approach the dais and turn the meeting over to the chair.
chapters.title: Staff opens Committee on Disabilities joint hearing

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please settle down.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We're about to begin shortly.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to the Committee on Disabilities, Joint with Civil and Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, we ask that you please silence all electronics.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to testify, please see one of the sergeant at arms in the back.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And at no point, please do not approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shahana Hanif introduces herself as chair of the Committee on Disabilities and describes her appearance. She welcomes attendees to the joint oversight hearing with the Committee on Civil and Human Rights on disability discrimination enforcement at CCHR.
chapters.title: Chair Hanif opens joint oversight hearing on CCHR disability enforcement

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Shahana Hanif, Chair of the Committee on Disability.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm a brown woman in my mid-30s with long black curly hair.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm wearing a red power suit and I'm seated behind the dais.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Welcome to today's joint oversight hearing with the Committee on Civil and Human Rights, where we will examine disability discrimination enforcement trends at the New York City Commission on Human Rights, or CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to Chair Nurse for partnering with us on this important hearing.

chapters.summary: Hanif notes millions of New Yorkers live with disabilities and disability is now the most common basis of claims filed with CCHR. She says strong protections on paper mean little if New Yorkers cannot access them in practice.
chapters.title: Hanif frames disability discrimination as most common CCHR claim

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Millions of New Yorkers live with disabilities, and disability discrimination is now the most common basis of claims filed with CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: New York City has some of the strongest civil rights protections in the country.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Our human rights law provides broader protections for people with disabilities than state or federal law, including the right to reasonable accommodations and a good faith cooperative dialogue with employers, landlords,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: and businesses and their accessibility needs.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But strong protections on paper mean very little if New Yorkers cannot access them in practice.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Rights without meaningful enforcement are promises unfulfilled.

chapters.summary: Hanif describes a CCHR ruling involving a tenant who spent more than four years requesting a ramp or lift and died before it was installed. She says accessibility delayed is accessibility denied and delays can have irreversible consequences.
chapters.title: Hanif recounts tenant who died waiting for ramp accommodation

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In August, CCHR issued a ruling in a case involving a tenant who spent more than four years requesting a ramp or lift so he could safely leave his apartment.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Tragically, he died before that accommodation was ever installed.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: A disabled New Yorker spent years fighting for the basic ability to leave his own home.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: He died before that right was realized.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Accessibility delayed is accessibility denied.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And in some cases, those delays have irreversible consequences.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This is precisely why today's hearing matters.

chapters.summary: Hanif says a December 2025 state comptroller audit found housing discrimination cases took over two years on average. She notes CCHR does not publicly report how long disability cases take or what outcomes complainants receive.
chapters.title: Hanif cites comptroller audit and CCHR data on aging caseload

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: A December 2025 audit by the New York State Comptroller found that the housing discrimination cases reviewed took more than two years, on average, to reach a determination.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: CCHR's own data also show an aging caseload, yet the agency does not publicly report how long disability discrimination cases take to resolve

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: or what outcomes complainants ultimately receive.

chapters.summary: Hanif lists questions about CCHR's 2026 reorganization, implementation of comptroller recommendations, coordination with MOPD, translation of guidance into enforcement, and needed resources or reforms. She says the hearing will also cover four pieces of legislation.
chapters.title: Hanif outlines oversight questions on intake, backlog, coordination, and resources

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Today, we intend to examine several critical questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: One, how will CCHR's 2026 reorganization improve intake, investigations, and resolution timelines for disability discrimination complaints?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Two, what concrete steps has the agency taken to implement the state comptroller's recommendations and address its growing backlog?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Three, how are CCHR and the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities coordinating to ensure complaints are addressed effectively and that New Yorkers are not left navigating fragmented systems?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Four, how is CCHR translating?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It's updated disability discrimination guidance into meaningful enforcement, education, and compliance.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And finally, what additional resources, data, transparency, or policy reforms are necessary to ensure that New Yorkers receive timely relief?

chapters.summary: Hanif describes Intro 131, sponsored by Council Member Tiffany Caban, to amend the definition of gender in the Human Rights Law. She also introduces Intro 1107, which she sponsors, to require guidance and public education on service animal access.
chapters.title: Hanif introduces Intro 131 and Intro 1107

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We will also hear four pieces of legislation that advance our city's commitment to civil rights, accessibility, and disability justice.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Intro 131, sponsored by Councilmember Tiffany Caban, would amend the definition of gender under the New York City Human Rights Law.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Intro 1107, which I am proud to sponsor, would require guidance and public education regarding service animal access in places of public accommodation.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And that bill is particularly important as CCHR recently reached a settlement with the MTA following allegations of harassment and discrimination against people traveling with service animals on city buses.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This legislation seeks to make existing protections clearer and more accessible to the public and businesses alike.

chapters.summary: Hanif describes Reso 510, sponsored by Council Member Julie Won, to declare June 18 Autistic Pride Day. She also introduces Reso 665, which she sponsors, calling on the U.S. Senate to ratify the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
chapters.title: Hanif introduces Reso 510 and Reso 665

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: RESO 510, sponsored by Councilmember Julie One, would declare June 18 Autistic Pride Day in New York City, recognizing and celebrating autistic New Yorkers and their contributions to our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And finally, RESO 665, which I'm also proud to sponsor, calls on the United States Senate to approve and the President to ratify the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the People.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: the rights of persons with disabilities and its optional protocol as we mark the convention's 20th anniversary.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The convention affirms that disability rights are human rights and that people with disabilities deserve full and equal participation in every aspect of society.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: 20 years after its adoption, the United States still has not ratified it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That failure is long overdue for correction.

chapters.summary: Hanif acknowledges Council Members Caban and Epstein and thanks the administration, advocates, service providers, and public. She thanks committee staff including Sarah Sucher, Chloe Rivera, Emma Teran, Simone Lavin, and Teyuta Muai.
chapters.title: Hanif acknowledges colleagues, administration, advocates, and staff

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge my colleagues who have joined us, Councilmember Tiffany Caban, Councilmember Harvey Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to the administration for being here today and to the disability advocates, service providers, healthcare workers, and members of the public who have come to testify or submitted written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Your presence here is an act of self-advocacy, and we do not take it for granted.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to the committee staff who have made today's hearing possible, including Senior Legislative Counsel

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Sarah Sucher and Senior Legislative Policy Analyst Chloe Rivera, my Senior Advisor Emma Teran, Communications Director Simone Lavin, and Legislative Fellow Teyuta Muai.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And now I will turn it over to Chair Nurse for her opening remarks.

chapters.summary: Council Member Sandy Nurse, chair of Civil and Human Rights, thanks co-chair Hanif and notes disability is the most common basis of claims. She says CCHR is a small agency with a large mandate and its work is an issue of economic justice.
chapters.title: Chair Nurse opens with CCHR mandate and economic justice

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Happy Friday.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: My name is Sandy Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm chair of the Civil and Human Rights Committee.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I want to start by first thanking my co-chair, Councilmember Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And as she just mentioned in her own opening statement, the Commission on Human Rights

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Rights has reported that disability is the most common basis of claims filed amongst protected classes.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Something I wish to emphasize for everyone here is that CCHR is a relatively small agency tasked with a very large mandate.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We totally recognize that.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It is the enforcement agency for one of the most expansive human rights laws in the country.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Perhaps most importantly, the people they serve often don't have any other way to enforce their rights because they may not be able to afford a private attorney, so CCHR's work is also very much an issue of economic justice.

chapters.summary: Nurse responds to the story of a tenant who died waiting for an accommodation and says justice delayed is justice denied. She hopes the hearing will show how CCHR resources and structure affect access to housing, employment, and daily necessities.
chapters.title: Nurse says justice delayed is justice denied and highlights reorganization

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The heartbreaking story that Chair Hanif shared about someone who died while waiting years for a disability accommodation emphasizes something we already know to be true, which is that justice delayed is justice denied.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: That is why our main goals today are so important.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We hope this hearing will shine a light on how CCHR's resources and organizational structure have real,

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: tangible impacts on how people with disabilities can enjoy access to secure housing, employment, and day-to-day necessities without discrimination or undue disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: My co-chair noted CCHR's recent reorganization, something that I'm hoping will be able to positively impact its workflows, and this is something we've discussed in multiple hearings before,

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: and especially how quickly people can have their complaints resolved.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: At the end of the day, that is what's most important, is that there is relief.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: for those facing discrimination and hardships due to discrimination.

chapters.summary: Nurse says discrimination can have a detrimental snowball effect, such as someone unable to leave home then losing work. She says some situations become emergencies that cost people their health or lives.
chapters.title: Nurse describes snowball effects of discrimination and emergency harms

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: For a lot of New Yorkers, these issues impact their lives on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: They often have a detrimental snowball effect.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: For example, someone unable to leave their home due to a lack of a possible accommodation may then be unable to get to work, lowering their income and starting a series of events.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: At times in emergency situations, it can cost them their life or their health.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I recognize that not every situation is this dire, but we still believe it's important to know that some situations are and many have the potential to get to that point.

chapters.summary: Nurse says she is curious how CCHR responded to the comptroller audit and how internal changes affect resolution times. She looks forward to hearing about CCHR's disability enforcement, education, testing, and work with MOPD.
chapters.title: Nurse asks how CCHR responded to comptroller audit and MOPD coordination

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm curious how CCHR has responded to the Comptroller's audit mentioned by my co-chair and how any internal changes are impacting resolution times.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from the Commission on its disability-related enforcement, education, and testing, and also hope to learn more about its dynamic and work with MOP.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: PD in order to better serve New Yorkers as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I want to thank everyone here who's come and made it here today on Friday, everyone who worked on this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm grateful for everybody who's going to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I believe we're now going to hear from Councilmember Caban on her bill.

chapters.summary: Council Member Tiffany Caban introduces herself and thanks Chairs Nurse and Hanif for holding the hearing. She says as a New Yorker with chronic illness she is grateful for their leadership and that her bill Intro 131 protects intersex New Yorkers from discrimination.
chapters.title: Caban introduces Intro 131 on intersex protections

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: My name is Councilmember Tiffany Caban.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I am a Puerto Rican woman with a ponytail and glasses and wearing a beige sweater.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to thank Chairs Nurse and Hini for holding this important hearing on disability and discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: As a New Yorker myself with chronic illness, I'm grateful for your leadership in making our city more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I also want to thank the two of you for giving me time in this hearing for my bill, which does not neatly fit into the theme of this hearing, but which is nonetheless crucial to many New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Caban says Intro 131 would ensure the human rights law protects intersex New Yorkers. She thanks Interact and directly impacted people for working on the legislation and describes discrimination, denial of health care, and hate violence faced by intersex people.
chapters.title: Caban details intersex discrimination and thanks Interact

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 131, would ensure that our city's human rights law protects intersex New Yorkers from discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Before I describe that legislation, I just want to deeply, deeply thank the folks at Interact.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We have the executive director, Erica, here, as well as Liat Feller, Jen Levine, Alicia Roth-Weigel, Alyssa Ball.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Brian E.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Price, and I remember meeting with students to work on this piece of legislation, Intersex Students, and it represents the best of what

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: government governing and being in partnership with community should be.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Directly impacted people coming to their elected officials and saying where the government needs to step up to protect them.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So, you know, it's been clear to folks in the LGBTQIA plus community that for too long, intersex people have faced bigotry and discrimination, been denied the health care that they need, and have been subjected to hate violence.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And the federal government has at best failed to protect intersex people, and that's putting it in the mildest, kindest terms.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And under this administration specifically,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: has made it difficult for many intersex people to obtain documents reflecting an ex-gender marker.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that's why it's...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: all the more important that our city enforce anti-discrimination laws to keep intersex New Yorkers safe, enable them to access the care that they need, and protect them from discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So again, thank you, and I'll pass it back to the chairs.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif reads a statement from Council Member Julie Won supporting Resolution 510. The statement thanks Chairs Hanif and Nurse and credits autistic self-advocate Gary Oye-Steven for sparking the bill.
chapters.title: Hanif reads Julie Won statement on Autistic Pride Day

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And now I will read a statement that was provided by my colleague, Councilmember Julie Wan, on her bill.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs Hanifa Nurse, for convening this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm honored to have my bill, Resolution 510, heard at this hearing for the Committee on Disabilities and Committee on Civil and Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This resolution will declare June 18th annually as Autistic Pride Day in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to take a moment to thank Gary O.E.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Stephen, whose outreach and advocacy was the spark that got this bill drafted.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Gary, an autistic self-advocate and a proud New Yorker, reached out to my office because he believed this city should formally recognize this day, and he is right.

chapters.summary: The statement says autism presents differently for every person and no one should be reduced to a diagnosis. It describes how Aspies for Freedom created Autistic Pride Day in 2005 as a counter to Autism Awareness Month narratives.
chapters.title: Hanif reads statement on autism diversity and Autistic Pride Day history

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Autism spectrum disorder presents differently for every single person, and no two individuals share the same experience, and no one should be reduced to a diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And yet for too long, public conversation around autism has done exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That's exactly why Autistic Pride Day exists.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In 2005, an organization called Aspies...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: For freedom, led by autistic individuals, created this day.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: They didn't wait for someone else to speak on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: They built a space for self-determination, for neurodiversity, for pride.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And they did.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: did it deliberately as a counter to the Autism Awareness Month narrative, which was too often led by non-autistic voices, too often centered on deficits, on fixing, on curing.

chapters.summary: The statement says autism and neurodivergence are not problems to be solved but communities to celebrate. It describes the rainbow infinity symbol and says Reso 510 would declare June 18 Autistic Pride Day in New York City.
chapters.title: Hanif reads statement on rainbow infinity symbol and bill purpose

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I want to make it clear, autism and neurodivergence is not a problem to be solved, but instead a community to be celebrated.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The symbol of this day is a rainbow infinity sign, which is fitting to embody the infinite diversity, potential, and future of the autism and neurodivergent community.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This is why my bill, Reso 510, will declare June 18th annually as Autistic Pride Day in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This bill will make sure that this community that is far too often neglected or unsupported will get the recognition, respect, and visibility they deserve.

chapters.summary: The statement thanks Autistic Adults NYC, Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled, Autistic Self-Advocacy Network, AHRC, and New York Lawyers for the Public Interest. It says recognizing the day affirms that institutions and communities are stronger when they include neurodivergent individuals.
chapters.title: Hanif reads thanks to disability organizations supporting Reso 510

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to Autistic Adults NYC, Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled, Autistic Self-Advocacy Network, AHRC, and New York Lawyers for the Public Interest for their support on this resolution.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: By recognizing this day, our New York City institutions, workplaces, and communities can affirm they are stronger when we include neurodivergent individuals.

chapters.summary: Hanif calls Deputy Commissioner JoAnn Kamuf Ward, Assistant Commissioner Stephanie Rivera, and Deputy Commissioner Belkis Morig to be sworn. Staff asks them to raise their right hands and affirm to tell the truth.
chapters.title: Hanif administers oath to CCHR and MOPD witnesses

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Now the Committee Council will administer the oath to Deputy Commissioner for Policy and Legislative Affairs at CCHR, Joanne Kamif-Ward, I'm sorry if I mispronounced your name, Assistant Commissioner for Pre-Complaint Intervention and Litigation at CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Stephanie Rivera, and Deputy Commissioner and Senior Legal Officer at MOPD, Belkis Marig, members of the administration prior to their testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Will you please raise your right hand and verbally respond with, I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when ready.

chapters.summary: JoAnn Kamuf Ward, Deputy Commissioner for Policy and Legislative Affairs at CCHR, thanks the committees and introduces Stephanie Rivera and Belkis Morig. She underscores CCHR's commitment to ensuring New Yorkers with disabilities can live free from discrimination.
chapters.title: JoAnn Kamuf Ward introduces CCHR and MOPD panel

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Hanif and Chair Nurse and members and staff of the Committees on Disability and Civil and Human Rights, as well as members of the public who made the time to come today.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Thank you so much for convening today's hearing on disability protections and enforcement.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: As referenced, my name is Joanne Kama Ford.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Perfect pronunciation, Joanne.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: My role at the commission is Deputy Commissioner for Policy and Legislative Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And as noted, I'm joined by Stephanie Rivera, our Assistant Commissioner for Pre-Complaint Intervention and Litigation in the commission's newly renamed Office of Civil Rights Enforcement,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: as well as Balkees Mirig, Deputy Commissioner and Senior Legal Officer from the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I just want to start by underscoring the Commission's commitment to ensuring that New Yorkers with disabilities can live, work, access services, and participate fully in our city free from discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: As noted, disability protections comprise a significant part of the Commission's work.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: significant part of the Commission's work, and CCHR uses a range of tools, including education, outreach, investigations, and litigation to prevent and remedy discrimination.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says CCHR uses education, outreach, investigations, and litigation to prevent and remedy discrimination. She explains CCHR investigates complaints, resolves matters before formal complaints, and develops Know Your Rights materials.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward gives overview of Human Rights Law disability protections

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Today, I'll provide a brief overview of the City Human Rights Law's disability protections, as well as enforcement and outreach.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: More details on the specifics are in my written testimony.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: CCHR's enforcement includes investigating complaints as well as seeking to resolve matters before a formal complaint is filed where appropriate and securing remedies for violations of the law.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The Commission also provides trainings and develops Know Your Rights and Know Your Obligations materials so that New Yorkers and covered entities understand their rights and responsibilities under the City Human Rights Law.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: These functions complement one another.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Community engagement promotes awareness of the law and access to the commission, while our enforcement removes barriers to accessibility and protects the rights of persons with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Our engagement and enforcement support the end goals of attaining individual remedies and preventing future discrimination.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says the Human Rights Law prohibits discrimination in work, housing, and public places and requires reasonable accommodations absent undue hardship. She says accommodations can include policy changes, workplace adjustments, ramps, or lifts and require a cooperative dialogue.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward explains reasonable accommodations and cooperative dialogue

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The Human Rights Law aims to achieve independent and equal access to all aspects of city life for New Yorkers and broadly protects people with disabilities from discrimination at work, in their living spaces, and in public places.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: To this end, the law prohibits employers, housing providers, and places of public accommodation from discriminating against individuals because of an actual or perceived disability.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Service providers and housing providers must ensure full and equal enjoyment of their facilities and services, regardless of disability, and employers are prohibited from treating employees less well on the basis of disability.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The city human rights law also requires covered entities to provide reasonable accommodations for people with disabilities unless doing so would impose an undue hardship.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: An accommodation may include changes to policies or practices, workplace adjustments, or the installation of ramps or lifts to make a building accessible.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: As noted, part of the process of providing a reasonable accommodation is the obligation to have a cooperative dialogue with an individual to help identify their needs and how to meet them.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says disability claims were the most common type of claim in FY26 across employment, housing, and public accommodations. She describes pre-complaint interventions, Project Equal Access, and testing as tailored enforcement tools.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward describes enforcement tools and FY26 disability claims

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: CCHR uses various enforcement tools so the agency can respond to the circumstances of individual matters and where appropriate address broader patterns of potential discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In fiscal year 26, disability claims were the most common type of claim across the areas of employment, housing, and public accommodations, which is similar to recent years'trends.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The claims filed and formal complaints lead to an investigation by the agency's Office of Civil Rights Enforcement.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In order to remove barriers faced by individuals with disabilities and foster inclusive and accessible spaces, the Commission employs tailored approaches in addition to complaint investigations and litigation.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The Commission may, for example, use pre-complaint interventions, which we'll call PCIs, to seek timely resolution.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: before a formal complaint is filed.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Where physical accessibility is at issue, the Commission has a team, Project Equal Access, that works with housing providers and businesses to identify how to make spaces accessible, delivering faster solutions to persons with disabilities,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: including grab bars, ramps, and lifts.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says violations can lead to modifications, policy changes, damages, and civil penalties. She highlights FY26 resolutions including a ramp installation and $122,000 in emotional distress damages plus back rent.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward details remedies and case outcomes

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: CCHR also proactively identifies potential discrimination through testing to assess compliance with the human rights law and a range of areas which include identifying potential barriers to accessibility.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Together, pre-complaint interventions, testing, and resolution of individual complaints are critical for securing meaningful relief and promoting compliance with the city human rights law.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: When the Commission identifies violations of the law, covered entities may need to take actions such as modifications or policy changes and can also be ordered to pay damages to individuals and to pay civil penalties.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The agency may also seek remedies to prevent future discrimination and promote an accessible city.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In employment and public accommodations, respondents can be required to create reasonable accommodation policies and post notices so employees and patrons know their rights.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward describes another case where housing providers agreed to 14 months of rental credit and an accessible apartment transfer. She says CCHR couples enforcement with Human Rights Law 101 trainings and community partnerships.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward highlights housing resolutions and education work

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I want to highlight that in fiscal year 26, case resolutions also played a role in ensuring New Yorkers with disabilities were able to access their housing.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We heard about one example already.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In another matter, the commission was able to assist an individual whose landlord had refused to enter into a cooperative dialogue or in

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: install a ramp after their mobility became limited.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: As a result, the tenant had to stay longer than needed in a rehab facility because he could not enter his building.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The commission ultimately secured an agreement to compel the housing provider to build a ramp, and the complaint was awarded $122,000 in emotional distress damages as well as reimbursed back rent.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In another matter, housing providers that failed to accommodate an individual ultimately agreed to provide 14 months of rental credit and to transfer the individual to an accessible apartment.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: These case outcomes demonstrate that disability enforcement resolutions are tailored for an array of circumstances.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says CCHR works with community organizations, advocates, elected officials, businesses, and housing providers. She mentions the Disability Unite Festival and Disability Pride Parade as examples of outreach with MOPD and the Public Advocate.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward describes outreach and Disability Unite Festival

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: CCHR's enforcement, I also want to note, is coupled with educating New Yorkers about the city human rights law in order to prevent discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The agency provides disability rights education through its Human Rights Law 101 trainings and through more focused programming.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The Commission also works with community-based organizations, disability advocates, elected officials, businesses, housing providers, and other partners to increase awareness of the law.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Community engagement helps New Yorkers recognize potential discrimination and allows CCHR to reach communities through trusted partners, which includes bringing information about rights and resources directly into neighborhoods across the city.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In fiscal year 26, the Commission continued to leverage community partnerships to advance the agency's mandate through events large and small.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: CCHR again partnered with Project Access for

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: to host the Disability Unite Festival, working with MOPD and the Public Advocates Office, and participated in the Disability Pride Parade, supporting the rights of New Yorkers living with disabilities to thrive in New York City.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: These are just some of the examples of our work to tackle disability discrimination.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says CCHR supports the explicit reference to intersex traits in Intro 131, consistent with existing interpretation and guidance. On Intro 1107, she says CCHR supports the intent but the administration is still reviewing which agency should lead.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward comments on Intro 131 and Intro 1107

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Now I'm going to turn to the bills that are being heard today.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The Commission appreciates the opportunity to comment on legislation before the committees concerning disabilities and civil rights protections.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: First, starting with Intro 131, the proposed legislation would amend the city human rights law definition of gender to expressly include sex characteristics, including intersex traits.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The Commission supports the explicit reference to intersex traits, which is consistent with CCHR's existing interpretation of the human rights law, the Commission's rules of practice, and our legal enforcement.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: guidance.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I will note this is not in my testimony, but the agency has been working with the law department and others in the city, including MOERJ, to really take strong stances against the federal tax on gender

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: identity protections and the move to isolate binary gender identities.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We can talk about that or not in the future.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Second, Intro 1107.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: This proposed legislation involves several agencies and calls for public information and guidance concerning the rights of individuals with service animals and the obligations of covered entities.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: CCHR supports the intent.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: of the legislation to raise awareness of anti-discrimination protections and relevant city, state, and federal codes.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The administration, including the law department and sibling agencies, are continuing to review this legislation and discuss the appropriate agency for this to be designated to complete if this bill moves forward.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says CCHR remains committed to ensuring New Yorkers with disabilities understand and can exercise their rights. She says covered entities must know their responsibilities and meaningful remedies must be available when discrimination occurs.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward closes with commitment to disability rights enforcement

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: To close, I'll just underscore again, the Commission remains committed to ensuring New Yorkers with disabilities understand and can exercise their rights, and that covered entities know their responsibilities and that meaningful remedies are available when discrimination occurs.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We appreciate the Council's time and attention and look forward to answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is MOPD justifying?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the committees will go into questions and acknowledges Council Member Rita Joseph has joined. She says they will kick off with questions for MOPD.
chapters.title: Hanif moves to questions and acknowledges Council Member Joseph

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, we'll go into questions then.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Rita Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Sweet.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what MOPD is responsible for when a New Yorker reports disability discrimination and when CCHR takes over. Belkis Morig says CCHR has prime purview, MOPD is not an enforcement agency, and MOPD refers discrimination complaints to CCHR or Project Equal Access.
chapters.title: Hanif asks MOPD role versus CCHR in discrimination complaints

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, we're going to kick off with some questions for MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I know that we are joined by Deputy Commissioner Belkis.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Am I pronouncing your name right?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, so to kick off, when a New Yorker reports disability discrimination in employment, housing, or public accommodation, what is MOPD responsible for?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And when does CCHR take over?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And this is to just better understand and get clarity on the relationship that MOPD has with CCHR as it pertains to these kinds of cases.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Haney, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: When, generally speaking, CCHR has prime purview over discrimination complaints, so if someone, for example, calls 311 and alleges discrimination, those are directly routed to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We do not, we're not an oversight or enforcement agency, so we don't enforce discrimination complaints.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: However, constituents can contact us directly.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We have a form on our website.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We have a phone line.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We also have ASL direct and email.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And so there are various ways that people in the disability community get in touch with MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And when an individual alleges discrimination, we refer them to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Sometimes, you know, if the complaint is a physical accessibility complaint, we'll directly refer them to Project Equal Access if it's applicable in that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And then we get a...

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: wide variety of other types of phone calls that aren't appropriate to refer to CCHR and we provide, you know, if businesses contact us about accessibility, we'll provide resources and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: So we serve, you know, as the voice of the disability community in City Hall and we provide resources to businesses, the general public, and anyone who contacts us with specific questions.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether MOPD can share how many people filled out its form or called its phone line. Morig says the phone line is busy but the prior administration did not track calls and MOPD has referred at least 22 alleged discrimination claims to CCHR since July.
chapters.title: Hanif asks how many New Yorkers contacted MOPD

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Now, are you able to share how many New Yorkers filled out the form or reached MOPD through the phone line, which is separate from the 311 line?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are you able to share how many constituents contacted MOPD regarding...

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We receive quite a few calls.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Our phone line is quite busy.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: When I was walking here this morning, our constituent services person was on the phone, and I couldn't say hi or bye.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: So we get quite a few phone calls.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: In the prior administration, that information was not tracked.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We're currently, we hired a new constituent services person in early July, and we've started to centralize the types of calls we receive.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We receive a wide, diverse range of calls, and so we're looking into centralizing that information and recording it so we have a better understanding of the types of questions and inquiries that we receive.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: So we don't have a number to share, unfortunately, today.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: But what I can say is that since July,

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: I don't have that number on hand, but I know that we've at least referred 22 alleged discrimination claims to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then is that similar for the form that you shared about?

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, sometimes it's a request for the commissioner to speak.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Like, we just have a general contact form on our website, and so those could be anything that anybody wants to reach us for.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks broadly what requests MOPD receives. Morig says the bulk of inquiries relate to housing, including physical accessibility and eviction threats, and MOPD generally refers those to CCHR.
chapters.title: Hanif asks what requests come through MOPD hotline and forms

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then broadly, could you share what requests are coming through the hotline number and the forms?

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Yes, the bulk of the inquiries that we get are related generally to housing.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Housing tends to be, you know, the most challenging area for New Yorkers with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Often, you know, the questions are, you know, a combination of physical accessibility or housing discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Someone's facing eviction because of their disability or that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And we generally refer those directly to CCHR.

chapters.summary: Hanif notes CCHR's FY25 report highlighted collaboration with MOPD but FY26 did not mention MOPD. Kamuf Ward and Morig describe joint resources for small businesses, trainings, Disability Service Facilitator trainings, and outreach events.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about MOPD-CCHR collaboration and annual report omission

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: CCHR's fiscal year 2025 annual report highlights strengthened collaboration with MOPD, but its fiscal year 2026 report does not mention MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What specifically can you share about that collaboration and what it achieved and what does its ongoing work look like?

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think just to say on the annual report that it's a snapshot of activities, but definitely not everything.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: In the kind of past year, fiscal year 26, but really beginning.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In fiscal year 25, we worked with MOPD to create a number of updated resources for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So information on small business accessibility that live on the both MyCity page.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: which is SBS's resource for small businesses, as well as developing kind of joint training programs.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Again, many focused on small businesses.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So those are a couple of areas of collaboration so far.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think as Deputy Commissioner from MOPD mentioned, we also are referring cases internally across agencies and thinking, I think, always about ways to work together.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Of course, do outreach events like the Disability Unite Festival that I mentioned, the SBS Small Business Expo, and I think the Deputy Commissioner from MOPT has a few other MOPD-sponsored events that we participated in.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Yeah, we...

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We collaborated with CCHR on the disability service facilitators trainings, for example.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We had one on fair housing earlier this, I think in June.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And then I think last year we had a source of income training.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: So we convened the DSFs of various agencies for trainings.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: CCHR attended our Deaf Town Hall, which we held very recently.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And I believe we've had a couple of...

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We've tabled a lot next to each other, but generally we're, you know, lines of communications are open and we generally work together, especially for outreach events.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether referrals to CCHR have improved. Kamuf Ward describes warm handoffs to Project Equal Access, and Stephanie Rivera explains that Project Equal Access does site visits and may already have an open confidential matter.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about referral outcomes and warm handoffs

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And then when it comes to cases that are being referred to CCHR, were there any...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: outcomes or improvements in that area that you all have engaged on together to make that process maybe easier.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In terms of complaint referrals?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I mean, I think just what we're saying is where possible, doing a warm handoff between agencies.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So if the team at MOPD hears something and they can then reach out directly to Project Equal Access, and we have the deputy, the assistant commissioner who oversees that team here, so you can speak in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Excuse my voice.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I do directly oversee Project Equal Access, which is the team of individuals that do basic outreach in the community when we receive a complaint of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: They are in the fields on the streets assessing whether accommodations and modifications are essentially feasible for those individuals.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so often we receive referrals directly from MLPD in which Project Equal Access will then do site visits and meet with those individuals in their homes or in those public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Some of those cases do end up in filed complaints.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But what I do see right now is that many times those individuals are reaching out to multiple agencies at once.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we may already have an open matter for that individual.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we'll advise MOPD that there is an existing case.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But because...

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: It is open.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: It is considered confidential.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So a lot of our collaboration has to take a pause on those matters.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many staffers work solely on Project Equal Access. Rivera says the team has three members, with one recently added in the reorganization, and other intervention staff handle non-physical reasonable accommodation requests.
chapters.title: Hanif asks how many staff are dedicated to Project Equal Access

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how many staffers are dedicated solely to Project Equal Access?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Project Equal Access has three members.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: One was recently added in the reorganization, although pre-complaint interventions for individuals with disabilities can run the gamut.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we do have other staff members in our intervention work that focus on reasonable accommodation requests that do not require some sort of physical modification.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And we'll come back to a few more questions about Project Equal Access.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks for a breakdown of the 22 referrals by employment, housing, and public accommodations. Kamuf Ward says she does not have the breakdown but believes most were housing, and agrees to follow up after the hearing.
chapters.title: Hanif asks for breakdown of MOPD referrals and tracking

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, you mentioned that 22 cases were referred to CCHR regarding a disability-related issue.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are you able to give us a breakdown of how many concerned employment, housing, public accommodations, or any other issue areas?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have that breakdown in front of me, but I believe the bulk of them were housing that we referred, and that's the majority of the complaints that we receive.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then can we follow up with you to get that breakdown after this hearing?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Sure.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks for more detail on the warm handoff to CCHR. Kamuf Ward says people may contact Rivera or Project Equal Access directly, and CCHR tries to follow up with MOPD by email or phone and capture matters in its case management system.
chapters.title: Hanif asks how the referral handoff works

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And could you describe the referral handoff so that we have better clarity on...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Commissioner, you mentioned, Deputy Commissioner also mentioned that there's a warm handoff to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is that warm handoff going to Project Equal Access?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What's, please describe the process.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think it's going to depend and be kind of sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: People will reach out directly to Stephanie, who is the assistant commissioner overseeing Project Equal Access.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think there's also staff at MOPD who directly work with our Project Equal Access team, so they might reach out to the director of that team as well.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And then it's always our goal to follow up with MOPD to let MOPD know what happened with the case.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think we have worked.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We're improving our ability to track whether that is happening in every case, as the deputy commissioner from MOPD was saying.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Our internal system is something that we're continually improving, including as part of this reorganization.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But really, it's usually over email or a phone call to a member of the Project Equal Access team.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And then those matters are captured in our case management system.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether CCHR can share tracker data after the hearing and whether MOPD tracks whether CCHR resolves referred cases. Kamuf Ward says the annual report numbers come from an internal database being improved, and Morig says MOPD does not track every referral outcome.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about case management tracker and MOPD tracking outcomes

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And your case management system, there's a tracker you're seeing on the particular issue areas, which we would be able to have access to after this hearing?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So the numbers in our annual report are the numbers of all of the reports of discrimination that we get, including the referrals.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And that's like an internal database system, which is something that we are striving to improve by procuring a new case management system because some of the fields

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: make it hard to report out on the specifics of referrals and details of cases.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But that is the kind of basis of our annual report numbers, which is everything that comes to us as a matter.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then everything that MOPD referred out, are you all then tracking whether CCHR accepts and resolves these cases?

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: So as you know, we're a small office and we get, you know, hundreds of calls a month.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: So we don't track every individual call after we refer it.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: There are some where there's, you know, like project equal access cases.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We have a physical accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We have two.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Well, we're hiring a second, but we have physical accessibility specialists and they will directly contact CCHR's project equal access.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And for those cases, there is an exchange of information of, you know, and CCHR lets us know that they take it from here.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And generally speaking, unless the constituent comes back to us, we don't track eventual outcomes.

chapters.summary: Hanif recommends MOPD track outcomes for referred cases to ensure resolutions. She then passes questioning to Council Member Harvey Epstein, who has to leave.
chapters.title: Hanif recommends closing the loop on referrals and passes to Epstein

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I would make a recommendation that that kind of a tracking happens to close the loop, given folks are coming in through MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I think it's important that you're able to keep note that, okay, all of these 10 folks who were referred out to CCHR now have had...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Good resolution or two of them have not had any, have not heard back or something.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I don't know how, what that process would look like, but I think, uh,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: pretty significant to ensure that cases are resolved.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to pass it to Councilmember Epstein, who has to leave.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I also want to recognize that we've been joined by Councilmembers Hudson, Majority Leader Abreu.

chapters.summary: Epstein says housing discrimination cases are not being resolved quickly and a year is too long for people facing accessibility issues. Rivera says CCHR flags urgent matters for pre-complaint intervention and handles source of income and disability accommodation cases immediately.
chapters.title: Epstein asks how to expedite housing discrimination cases

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I can't stay long, but thank you for taking the time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can I just talk about housing discrimination issues?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Sounds like what we're hearing is someone calls a complaint, whether they're calling Mayor's Office of People with Disabilities or going directly to CCEHR.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: A year later, a lot of these cases are not being resolved.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And obviously someone who cares deeply about making sure people who have housing issues can get those resolved.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering how we get that system expedited.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What are we doing to help folks?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, this is truly a crisis for people, whether it's source of income discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if you don't get that resolved within a month, that apartment's gone.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If we're talking about other, you know, as the chair was talking about, accessibility issues, a year is a very long time for someone to sit and wait and suffer.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: That's actually really great, and I'm really honored to supervise our Project Equal Access team and our interventionists.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I will say at the point of contact with individuals, whether they're walking into our offices, being referred by other sibling agencies, or calling our live hotline,

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: we are flagging those matters as urgent matters and routing them for pre-complaint intervention.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And those are being handled immediately, whether it's lawful source of income or reasonable accommodations related to disabilities, which are the two areas I would say our interventionists are extremely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Deaf debt.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're able to secure housing quickly for individuals.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And when we are not, we are quickly filing those complaints, leveraging the expertise really of our interventionists in collecting evidence even before a complaint is filed.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so any situation where we believe we can get the accommodation that that household needs can be anywhere from a physical modification, like the installation of a ramp, right, which we know can take time.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Permits may be needed.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Landmarking may need to be consulted.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But generally, we are able to achieve those very quickly.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many source of income discrimination cases CCHR handled and how many resolved successfully. Rivera says she will get the numbers, and Kamuf Ward provides FY26 figures of 152 pre-complaint interventions and about 50 filed claims.
chapters.title: Epstein asks for source of income case numbers and outcomes

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So just on the source of discrimination cases, source of income discrimination, how many cases did you handle in the past year?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: For source of income discrimination, I will definitely get back to you on those specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And how many of those resolved successfully where the person actually said they deny me because I have Section 8, you know, you went to the landlord or the broker and said that's illegal and they got the department.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Could we get that data too?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely can get that data.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Again, I personally oversee that source of income emergency intervention team and knowing the results that we have been able to secure, including someone just last week, we were able to get fully housed with keys in hand, CityFAP's voucher holder, which we're very excited about.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And we're seeing those types of results on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Just so from my office, we get a lot of calls where people have city FEPS or they have a Section 8, and they're going through a thousand places and not getting the ability to get– they get turned down, turned down, turned down.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What I hear is they file complaints and they don't get those issues resolved.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So this is something we're seeing, obviously, as an affordability crisis in our city.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, 100%.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I just have some of the numbers, so I want to just respond to the questions.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So in pre-complaint interventions in fiscal year 26, 152 of those were lawful source of income

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: matters where we ultimately, what we call secure a housing opportunity, which can mean, you know, if someone was ghosted, they are able to see the apartment.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: If someone was denied an apartment, seeing if there's one available.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so those cases are definitely a priority.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: A complicating factor in source of income is that landlords are attacking the protection itself legally, and there's an ongoing court battle about state lawful source of income protections.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so we definitely see some housing providers less willing to come to the table for pre-complaint resolution, which requires someone to be willing to speak with us.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But where the pre-complaint intervention is not something that is successful, it moves on to a filed claim.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And we had about 50 of those in the lawful source of income space last year, but definitely a priority for this commissioner and for the assistant commissioner's team.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks whether delays are staffing-related or due to unresponsive landlords. Rivera says the team is fully staffed at six members and source of income pre-complaint closures averaged under 30 days, while Kamuf Ward describes the reorganization and new non-attorney investigators.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about timelines and staffing for source of income cases

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, and if you're able to move these quickly, that's great to know what that timeline is for those.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And also, if they're...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: aren't are those staffing related issues?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, is it they're not moving quick enough because you don't have a staff or you're not moving quickly enough because either you're not the landlord or broker is not responding or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: You know, we are a fully staffed team at six members.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're able to, on average, I believe our closure rates for pre-complaint interventions, particularly for lawful source of income, was under 30 days,

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: which is really impressive considering the current caseload of each interventionist who are also doing disability accommodations as well.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I just want to add to that because I think part of the kind of genesis of this hearing is talking also about a reorganization of

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: the agency, which is really to take as many resources as possible and move them into the frontline enforcement part of the agency.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So many of the pieces of cases historically have been handled by attorneys.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I'm an attorney.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Attorneys are wonderful, but they don't need to do every part of a case investigation.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so we have created a new role within our enforcement team, which are non-attorney investigators, to really help move the processes forward, which I think, you know, we can't say what the timelines are.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: This went into effect July 1.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But the goal is...

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Faster case processing times at every step so that in all protected categories we are moving cases faster.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and Eve and Sam.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Chair Nurse for letting me go out of turn.

chapters.summary: Hanif notes about a quarter of housing voucher users are New Yorkers with disabilities and asks how many complaints involve both disability and source of income discrimination. Kamuf Ward says CCHR does not have that breakdown but will follow up.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about overlapping disability and source of income complaints

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And just to build on Councilman Repstein's question, we know that approximately a quarter of people that use housing vouchers are New Yorkers with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How many complaints at CCHR involve both disability and source of income discrimination?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we don't have the breakdown of where we have both, but we can certainly follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We know that disability often is coupled with another protected category, be it source of income, race, gender.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so we can share that information and follow up.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then are these cases counted under both categories in CCHR's annual reporting?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It will actually depend on the specific matter because someone might come to us alleging source of income discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: They might be a person with a disability and they have a separate claim that way, or they might not be filing the claim.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So that's a kind of fact specific question.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many CCHR attorneys have significant experience in disability and source of income cases. Rivera says there are 13 staff attorneys without specific specialties, and says CCHR evaluates both protections and considers disparate impact of source of income policies.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about attorney experience and disparate impact cases

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And you were getting into discussing the kind of staffing structure of attorneys.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How many attorneys are at CCHR that have significant experience on these cases specifically in both areas?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We actually currently have 13 staff attorneys in our office.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Our attorneys handle all range of cases, so they don't necessarily have a specific specialty or topic or topic.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: area, our interventionists are really where the specialties are leveraged and how they communicate with respondents, negotiating tactics, and the nuances of the law before a complaint is filed.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then given that people with disabilities disproportionately rely on housing vouchers, has CCHR investigated whether source of income discrimination also constitutes disability discrimination?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
