utterances.text: And if so, has the agency pursued any disparate impact cases on that basis?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: That is accurate.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We often evaluate the incident or the alleged incident based off of both protections.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And we recognize, right, lawful source of income, it's very easy to only think about voucher discrimination, but that can include things like SSD benefits, which we know only individuals with disabilities are receiving.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so if they're denying or being denied the opportunity to view and apply for an apartment because of their use of those benefits, inherently we're going to automatically include both of those protected classes as a basis

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: and look at the desperate impact of policies that prohibit lawful source of income and how they impact those individuals.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'll pass it to Councilmember Nurse.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks why disability claims have increased. Rivera says people are choosing CCHR over federal or state forums, especially as civil rights are under attack, and CCHR does extensive disability rights outreach.
chapters.title: Nurse asks what is driving increase in disability claims

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about the complaint trends in the data.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: According to CTHR's annual reports, disability is the most common basis for claims, and we're seeing that in the last fiscal year, these claims increased.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Do you have a, you know, can you explain what you think is driving that increase?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: You know, the increase can definitely, we're seeing individuals choose our forum over federal or state forums right now, particularly when we know civil rights are publicly under attack.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We do extensive outreach and education work around disability rights in particular for individuals with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So we're often seeing that rise in that coordination and increased filed complaints and pre-complaint interventions.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Excuse me.

chapters.summary: Nurse notes 22 disability public accommodation claims reached filed complaints in FY26, up from 16. Rivera says it is underreporting, and CCHR also receives anonymous tips, including one that led to a commission-initiated action against Barnes & Noble.
chapters.title: Nurse asks whether public accommodation numbers show compliance or underreporting

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And so in the last fiscal year, 22 disability claims in public accommodations reached a filed complaint citywide, which is up from 16 from the year before.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Given how common and accessible storefronts, restaurants, issues in the public realm are, are you all reading that as compliance or underreporting?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Definitely an issue of reporting.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We know, again, that we are not the only forum individuals can...

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we are often, if we're not the first option or if they contact us and they've already reached out to other venues for options, right, we're not capturing those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Public accommodations is very unique in that we're also getting tips, particularly anonymous tips from individuals who are visiting New York City and want to say, hey, this is something that I experienced.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Can you investigate?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so oftentimes we're looking at those tips, seeing how we can convert them into other testing programs and possibilities for agency-initiated actions, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We know we had at least one commission-initiated action started in fiscal year 26 against Barnes& Noble, which did start based off of

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: tips about how heavy and inaccessible the entryway to that Barnes& Noble was in Union Square.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think, you know, I'll just add, because you mentioned it's often tips.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think we've heard already housing is a huge area of inquiries and complaints because it is necessary, right, for your daily life.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Public accommodations, for people to want to file a complaint, you really have to have the desire to sit through what can be a very unpleasant process.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We know that across protected categories.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So just underscoring, I don't think we see New York City as accessible.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But really the role we play in our corner is to try and address the individual discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: complaints that come to us, but definitely huge challenges.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how federal shifts affect dual filing agreements, disparate impact cases, and cooperation with the state human rights division. Kamuf Ward says CCHR stepped away from an EEOC dual filing contract to protect New Yorker data and continues to pursue disparate impact under city law.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about federal rollbacks, dual filing, disparate impact, and state cooperation

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And as you mentioned, we know the priorities for the federal government has shifted.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It seems like we don't have priorities for civil and human rights.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Can you speak to three areas of how this has impacted your work, specifically

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: when it comes to dual filing agreements, what happens instead?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And what is CCHR doing now that the federal government is not pursuing disparate impact cases?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And if you're now expanding cooperation with the state human rights divisions?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll start with just the federal government and the EEOC and HUD in particular.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So as you've noted, disparate impact is actually being taken away at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It is embedded into the city human rights law, so we will continue to pursue those cases.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But we did make a decision last year to step away from a contract with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I will say the contract that we had were for dual filing cases.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So if someone came to us, they would preserve a federal claim.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It was never enough money to sustain staffing at CCHR.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And we think the tradeoff of losing the small amount of money there is that we're protecting the identity of New Yorkers, right?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: If you're dual filing with the federal government, they can access your case data.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: That is something we don't feel comfortable with at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Individuals, though, can still choose to file federal claims in court or go directly to the EEOC.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we haven't, you know, I think it changes what people, the decisions people make when they come to us.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But generally, we think it's a net positive for New Yorkers that are filing.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think on just disparate impact, generally, I mentioned already some of the comments that we've been working on.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: They relate to HUD and disparate impact.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: They relate to HHS and gender and really seeking.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: ways to preserve what are the protections in the city human rights law.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think, you know, on the enforcement side, we have cases that are in litigation also addressing some of these claims.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And then just cooperation with the state human rights division.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think we have pursued that previously, but definitely in conversation more with the state, their resources have also grown and thinking about

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: not only on education and outreach, but potentially in the case arena, how we can collaborate.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: But nothing has been landed on yet.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We have been working on an MOU.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I don't know the exact status, but we are already sharing information in general on trends, and we do a lot of events together.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So there's a kind of ongoing partnership.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks whether employment disability complaints that would have been dual filed still reach a federal forum. Rivera says no, individuals must choose to go to the EEOC or federal court independently.
chapters.title: Nurse asks whether employment complaints can still reach federal forum

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Just want to acknowledge we've been joined by Councilmember Feliz Online.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And just related, do employment disability complaints that would have once been dual filed still reach a federal forum?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Yeah, you answered it a little bit, but...

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Ultimately, no, they will not be able to reach a federal forum if they file with us first.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: They would have to choose whether they want to go to the EEOC or federal court independently of us.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks what prompted the December 2025 disability guidance update and how CCHR operationalized it. Kamuf Ward says CCHR updated guidance on AI decision-making, made it shorter and broken down by jurisdiction, and expanded service animal guidance.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about 2026 reorganization and December 2025 disability guidance

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And so now I want to talk a little bit about the reorganization in 2026 and the December 2025 disability guidance.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: CCHR updated its guidance on disability protections in the HRL in December 2025.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Can you tell us what prompted this update and how CCHR has operationalized this guidance in handling disability cases?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think we've talked in some other spaces about other legal enforcement guidance.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It's generally part of our workflow that we are updating materials because cases change and what we're hearing from members of the public changes as well.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we...

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Have increasingly, like everyone and your colleagues, been thinking about AI and wanting New Yorkers to know that even if a housing provider, employer, or public accommodation is using a form of technology

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: in the decision-making chain that is still covered by the city human rights law, does not change liability, which is something that we added to the legal enforcement guidance.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We also updated the guidance to make it

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: shorter.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Lawyers, again,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: not their forte to make things shorter, but really to make it more accessible and break it down by area of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Previously, it was kind of everything was consolidated, which I think made it hard for people to understand if I'm in housing, what are my rights?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I'm a housing provider.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: What do I need to do?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And this is part of a move to also create more model policies for smaller businesses and housing providers, which don't have lawyers and HR to be doing that work.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think the other piece, which was in the guidance already, but which we built out a little bit, is around service animals and emotional support animals, because it's just a huge area of questions repeatedly coming to the agency.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks what substantive changes have occurred since the July restructuring. Kamuf Ward says CCHR moved staff into enforcement, doubled the InfoLine to 16 people, created investigator roles, and is developing new processing guidelines and a new case management system.
chapters.title: Nurse asks what changes followed the comptroller audit

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And in relationship to the Comptroller audit, which outlined a restructuring plan for July, now that we've had about three months, what substantive changes have you seen so far?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Or when do you expect those changes to affect case processing statistics?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think, you know, the thing that we have accomplished is moving a lot of staff into the enforcement unit.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So our Office of Civil Rights Enforcement, I think since last time I was in front of this committee, has our kind of info line, the first front line, has doubled in size.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So there's 16 people on that team now.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We've created a new role, an investigator role, so that when cases are found to be something CCHR

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: has jurisdiction over, there are more people on the team who are able to engage in the investigative steps, which allows the attorneys to be more focused on litigation, on settlements.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So the staffing piece is a huge part of what's happened.

chapters.summary: Kamuf Ward says it will take time to see case processing impacts and ideally next year or the year after. Rivera says InfoLine staff are being trained to draft complaints over the phone and CCHR is focusing on moving cases to OATH judges faster.
chapters.title: Kamuf Ward and Rivera detail reorganization and case processing changes

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think the other pieces that we have been revisiting is because the whole process is changing, we're developing new guidelines on processing and what these different roles at the agency

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: mean.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think, honestly, it will be a bit of time till we know what the impact on case processing times is, because we still have cases that have been with us that we are resolving.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I would say.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Ideally next year, maybe the year after we'll really see what the impact has been.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And then the third piece, which I

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I've already mentioned a little bit, is a new case management system that allows us both internally to better look at the data from cases and be able to report out that data, but is also more user-friendly for our staff.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But I don't know, Assistant Commissioner, a few things you want to add.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I was just going to touch on some of the action items that I'm actively working on with my team, both in InfoLine and the pre-complaint intervention stage, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: As the Deputy Commissioner mentioned, InfoLine has doubled to 16 members.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're currently training up all of those members to be able to draft legal complaints,

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: training them to take those complaints over the phone so that we can cut down on wait time and really bust open the front door, right, for how we file complaints.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And getting more done faster.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And then I would say, again, leveraging the expertise of our pre-complaint interventionists, particularly in disability and lawful source of income, so we can really streamline and fast-track how those investigations happen.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And then on the litigation side, as I said, I also get to supervise cases that move to the New York City Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings, and really focusing on how we, A, get more of our attorneys'cases

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: in front of Oath judges, cutting down on the number or the extent of settlement conferences, and moving quickly in front of those judges as well.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks whether CCHR expects to bring housing case processing back down to one year. Kamuf Ward says one year would be out of step with administrative agencies and courts, and case times depend on complexity and number of respondents.
chapters.title: Nurse asks whether housing case guidance will return to one year

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We love concrete actions being brought here.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So I know that during the audit period, you all had issued internal guidance in terms of housing case processing to a resolution from one year to two years.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Now that all of these things are in place, is this something that you expect to bring back down to one year?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I think our goals are always to move the cases as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think one year would be significantly out of step with both administrative agencies and court case times.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think we are hoping to route as many things into pre-complaint intervention as possible, but the challenge we always face with an average case time is that

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: we have the cases that run the gamut from one individual needing grab bars in an apartment to a building with multiple respondents, management companies, and many tenants.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so depending on the complexity of the case, it really will impact what the case times look like.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to echo that a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: You know, our cases and our investigative plans per case can really shift and change depending on the complexity of the case, how many witnesses we need to interview.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: how many documents, I mean, we need to issue, right, the number of respondents, even in a given case where we're identifying multiple bad actors, particularly

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: in the housing context where we're dealing with landlords, property management companies, brokers and their brokerages and salespeople, which can complicate and extend timeframes.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So I'm hearing that you will leave the guidance, internal guidance, to around two years for now.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think we will be doing our best to bring it down.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Aspirations, yes, I understood.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how CCHR measures impacts of expanded intake, outreach, investigations, and strategic enforcement. Kamuf Ward says meaningful resolutions are the North Star and CCHR will revisit metrics as staffing changes emerge.
chapters.title: Nurse asks how CCHR measures expanded capacity

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: You also reported, CCHR reported that OCRE significantly expanded capacity compared with the Law Enforcement Bureau in

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: intake, outreach, investigations, and strategic enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: How are you measuring the impacts of this expanded capacity in each area?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think the number one metric that we have always thought about is meaningful resolutions for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so I think that will continue to be the thing that we are using as our North Star in cases.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And, of course, looking at all the aspects of case processing time, as the assistant commissioner mentioned, you know, we ideally have no wait times.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: You come to us and we are serving you immediately.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: That is where we want to get.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But over, I think, as we see what these staffing changes emerge and look like, we'll be revisiting our MMR metrics and a whole host of kind of indicators to baseline over the next year.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how many of 12 mediation cases were disability cases and whether mediation is appropriate for accommodations. Rivera says five disability matters were referred to mediation and mediation can still secure accommodations and damages.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about mediation cases and disability matters

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, and then lastly on this topic, you all have expanded mediation.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I think you had 12 cases.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: How many of the 12 were disability cases?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And is mediation appropriate where the remedy is an accommodation, where the remedy is an accommodation the law already requires?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're actually very excited that our mediation program is expanding and adding members to the team.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Last fiscal year, we had five disability matters that were referred for mediation.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Because outcomes can still be achieved in mediation, whether that's getting a reasonable accommodation secured,

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: getting damages even still in those spaces, mediation is absolutely still appropriate so long as both parties are willing to meet at the table.

chapters.summary: Nurse thanks the witnesses and says she will return to questions later. She opens the floor to Council Member Caban for questions about her bill.
chapters.title: Nurse opens questioning to Caban

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to my questions in a little bit because I need my nose to have some time to recover.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I think we're going to open it up to Councilmember Caban.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Questions about your bill?

chapters.summary: Caban asks how often CCHR receives inquiries about discrimination against intersex people and why people may or may not report. Kamuf Ward says gender is a broad category and CCHR may not have specific intersex data, but recognizes intersex discrimination in materials and guidance.
chapters.title: Caban asks how often CCHR receives intersex discrimination inquiries

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you to the members of the administration that are here with us today.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm going to ask some questions about my bill, which, thank you, I really appreciate the testimony in support of the legislation, but particularly the words that you shared afterwards about

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: what this administration's commitment towards our communities are.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Discrimination against someone on the basis of intersex characteristics could intersect with a few different categories that CCHR reports, but it doesn't get recorded in its own category.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So how often does CCHR receive inquiries related to discrimination against someone who is intersex?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And do you have any thoughts around why or why not, in terms of why a person would?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: report or wouldn't report.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, so I'll start that, but I think feel free to add, Stephanie.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So, you know, one of, I think, the beautiful things about the city human rights law is its discrimination based on actual or perceived status.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: That means that not everyone has to come to us and tell us their particular gender identity.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Gender is a broad category that includes many...

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Has a quite expansive definition.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think we only need the details in some instances.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So if people claim gender discrimination, people could have reported that are intersex.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And we don't have that specific information, or to my knowledge, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I can follow up if that's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But I think in general, in answer to your question, we know that government has long been unfriendly to communities who don't fit into a gender binary, that has become readily apparent,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: more so as the federal government seeks to erase people's actual identities and denigrate them at every opportunity possible.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we do not fault people who don't feel comfortable coming to government, but we recognize that

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: seeing yourself and being represented in materials and examples is important for everybody so that they know they are seen and heard.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And as I mentioned in my testimony, you know, we have recognized.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: intersex discrimination in our public-facing materials, in our legal enforcement guidance, in our rules, recognizing that this is a significant issue that impacts people.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so it's incumbent on us and our sibling agencies, the Mayor's Office of LGBTQIA Affairs and Mayor's Office of Equity and Racial Justice, to be thinking about how we are making sure New Yorkers know we are there for them.

chapters.summary: Caban shares an example of a colleague who came out as intersex later in life and asks how CCHR handles such cases. Kamuf Ward says internal guidance already treats intersex discrimination as covered and cases go to the Office of Civil Rights Enforcement for factual interviews.
chapters.title: Caban asks how intersex discrimination cases are handled

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, it's interesting because I have a former colleague who is one of the most badass human rights lawyers,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: an outspoken and very public advocate for the queer community and only came out as intersex a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And you think about all of those things being true and what about the environment exists that creates the conditions where somebody like that, for example, doesn't come out until just now.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You've talked about this a little bit, but...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Somebody could call up with a complaint of gender discrimination, maybe not disclose that they're intersex.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But when you receive these cases, how do they get handled?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What's the CCHR's current legal guidance on the issue if you do learn?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, so our internal guidance is already that we would treat someone, if they were to call us and say, I think I've been

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: discriminated against in my workplace for being intersex, that could be being denied bathroom access, also in a public accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: That would go to the Office of Civil Rights Enforcement, who would do a factual interview just like they do in any other circumstance.

chapters.summary: Caban asks whether CCHR has heard feedback on shortcomings and whether it has trainings or materials on intersex issues. Kamuf Ward says Interact and Fordham Law Clinic raised the need for explicit statutory language and CCHR has a TGN-CBI training that can include this education.
chapters.title: Caban asks about feedback and trainings on intersex issues

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Have you heard any feedback from community partners or the public on shortcomings of the current protections provided under the human rights law?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I think we've heard from the same individuals that you've been working with interact, and I think the Fordham Law School Clinic, so I'm a Fordham alum, so shout out,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: on, again, what we're talking about right now, which is that some of the materials reference intersex persons, but it wasn't clearly articulated in the law.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so that, you know, is part of the calculation in supporting the legislation.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: There are, you know, many, many things in the city human rights law that I think advocates have come to us to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Associational discrimination is another area where some protected categories have protections because you are associated with a person related to their disability.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And that doesn't exist for every protected category.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So that's something we've been looking at as well.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And chairs, I just have one more question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So we know that the general public doesn't necessarily have a high level of awareness of what intersex status means or the challenges that people with intersex characteristics might face.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you have any specific trainings, materials, or outreach programming on this topic?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if you do, are those trainings or programs aimed at specific audiences?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Like, you know, an example would be medical providers, or is it for audiences at large?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, so we have a specific training that is on working with TGN-CBI people.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: in general that really has historically targeted employers, but we've offered it for many service providers, for colleagues at DOHMH and others.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So that is the natural place for kind of this type of education to exist.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But I think, you know, when discussing this bill, and if it passes, we will be in touch with the Mayor's Office of LGBTQIA Affairs to think about how do we get the word out.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So yeah, we're here to be partners in that, obviously interact and our student cohort are ready to be a part of that and looking forward to working together to make sure it gets passed.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether CCHR is working on reports about source of income and disability discrimination. Kamuf Ward says CCHR does educational materials and is working on a Renters' Rights Guide, and Hanif encourages more research on the intersection.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about reports on source of income and disability intersections

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Kavan.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to come back to the question around source of income discrimination and disability discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are there any reports in the works by CCHR on the topic?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I think in general, we do a lot of kind of educational materials, less kind of studies or reports on kind of trends that are happening.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We have a lot of nonprofit colleagues who are looking, and Source of Income in particular is one of those areas.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Unlock NYC is a close partner of the commission, but we have been thinking about and working on Renters'Rights Guide, which would cover kind of a host of these

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: protections and some of the ways that they intersect.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I would certainly love to see more just discourse and research on

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: the intersections between source of income discrimination and disability discrimination as something that's not getting enough attention and just the disproportionate amount of New Yorkers who are disabled, who are experiencing

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: a source of income discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I know in the past, CCHR would do these kinds of reports that did studies and really laid groundwork on the kind of narrative New York City should be thinking about on this topic.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So that's putting out an idea to you all.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether MOPD ever intervenes directly with landlords, employers, or businesses. Morig says MOPD engages landlords on physical accessibility and refers discrimination issues to CCHR, and is forming an interagency working group on elevator delays.
chapters.title: Hanif asks whether MOPD intervenes directly with landlords

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to come back to some questions for MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Does MOPD...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: ever intervene directly with landlords?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I know that you mentioned that you're mostly referring folks out to CCHR's team, but is there any,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: does your constituent liaison ever more directly do interventions, speaking to landlords directly or employers, businesses?

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: If a landlord reaches out to us about, for example, physical accessibility, we will engage with them and advise them.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We generally tell them to hire an accessibility specialist, but we'll provide guidance and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: But generally speaking, if there's a discrimination issue, we do refer that to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: There are some, you know, sometimes it's an elevator issue.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And for example, if it's in an HPD building, we'll, you know, get in touch with HPD and let them know.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Or DOB, depending on where, if a complaint has already been filed, like DOB is usually the first agency to be involved if an elevator is down.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: But we'll also follow up and flag with HPD if it's in an HPD building.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And so those are some of the circumstances where we might be involved with landlords that aren't related to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: But that's generally the universe of that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So case by case.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And are there, would you say that these kind of direct interventions lead to

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: resolutions like the elevator getting fixed or a landlord successfully

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: understanding what they're supposed to ensure renters with disabilities know or whatever hypothetical situation.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We don't have information on those that we've referred to CCHR, but we do know, for example, in the elevator context, this is a recurring issue.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: There are significant delays in getting elevators repaired.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And so we are actually in the process of working to form an interagency working group to address some of these recurring systemic issues.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: So that's something that we're exploring right now and elevators is.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Number one agenda item.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what other trends require interagency coordination and whether MOPD has made formal recommendations. Morig cites elevator issues and school bus curb cuts, and says MOPD has not made formal recommendations but collaborates with CCHR.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about other systemic trends and formal recommendations

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are there other trends or issues that is requiring this kind of interagency coordination?

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: I don't, I'm not, you know, I don't have trends in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We don't do that type of tracking, but there are, you know, the elevator issue is an obvious one that we see on a recurring basis.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And then there are some more complicated issues that require several agencies to work out, you know, a type of accommodation.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And so, you know, for example, we have issues with students who disembark from school buses in front of DOE schools.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: You know, DOE would like curb cuts in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: DOT has to be involved.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And so we bring the agencies together to work out solutions that address, you know, everyone's concerns and also get students safely into schools.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so I think the elevator example is a good one in where this kind of systemic intervention is necessary and this interagency coordination is rightfully being prioritized.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Has MOPD made other formal recommendations to CCHR or other agencies when it comes to specific other kinds of issues similar to the elevator and then the curb cuts in front of schools?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That's another good example where it's systemic.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, the curb cuts aren't a discrimination issue, but generally speaking, we work very closely with CCHR on referrals and accessibility and their general...

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: really very responsive.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We haven't made formal recommendations, but we're always collaborating and, you know, addressing and working together in public education, outreach, and that sort of thing.

chapters.summary: Rivera says long elevator outages trigger reasonable accommodation obligations and Project Equal Access advocates for repairs, apartment transfers, temporary placements, or rent credits. Kamuf Ward adds that accessible design for small businesses is another area of interagency work.
chapters.title: Rivera describes Project Equal Access work on elevator outages

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yeah, Chironi, if I can interject just to amplify again some of the work of Project Equal Access and the PCI team, right, elevator outages, we know frequent or long-term elevator outages has

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: obligations, right, for reasonable accommodations for individuals with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so oftentimes we do go out to the sites and see, A, if there are repairs needed, how quickly those repairs can be facilitated.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: If we know that this is an ongoing issue in an old building, we've advocated for apartment transfers.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We've had instances where buildings are actively doing elevator modernization, which does mean that elevators could be out for anywhere from six to 12 weeks and sometimes much longer.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And we've been able to advocate for temporary placements in other housing, hotels, or even individuals who want rent credits while they're outside of their apartment, if that's feasible.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we're always thinking about a robust, creative ways that we can make those individuals whole again and get to stay in their apartments for as long as possible.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: I think the other area I'll just flag for, I think, interagency collaboration harkens back to something I mentioned earlier, but really thinking about

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: accessible design, right, for small businesses or cafes and restaurants and thinking about how we collaborate with both our agencies collaborate with with SBS to support small businesses who are interested in

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: in accessibility on on the front end.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think a challenge is we've all

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: recognized and probably experienced with New York is even if you can make the front to a small store accessible, it's not always navigable inside.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so there's a lot of resources that can help on the front end address that in new buildings or spaces.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether CCHR has a mechanism to determine when a case is urgent and whether MOPD requests fast-tracking. Morig says MOPD flags urgent situations to Project Equal Access, and Rivera describes triage for physical harm, shelter, employment, and pregnancy cases.
chapters.title: Hanif asks how CCHR triages urgent cases

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And is there a mechanism where CCHR,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: determines when a constituent's case is urgent, more urgent than other cases?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And does MOPD, in its intervention or referral system,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: like a tenant who can't leave their apartment because there isn't a ramp, or a worker who could lose their job because of an accommodation, not having that accommodation of a ramp.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Does MOPD ever, during its intervention, request to CCHR, this needs to be fast-tracked?

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: If it's an urgent situation, we directly flag it to Project Equal Access.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: This is rare, but I'm aware of at least one situation where it was an emergency situation and our accessibility specialist did go on site to address the situation and to investigate.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yes, I also remember that case.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We do kind of have a triage a bit.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So we're thinking about whether someone is in physical harm for other cases.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: If they can't leave their home, access medical appointments, get food, we're always going to prioritize those cases.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Individuals who are in homeless shelters, we're going to prioritize supporting those cases and finding housing.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So we're constantly evaluating, even in the employment context, we're growing our pre-complaint intervention impacts right now in the employment space.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We recognize it's something that's very fact-specific, but our interventionists are being trained up in that manner as well.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So we're thinking about whether accommodation can help someone return to work quicker if they've been on leave or execute their job duties in a better way.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're also doing those interventions even for individuals who are pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And even though we do have that as a separate protected class, we're also intervening in those matters because that's a temporary situation for that person, for that pregnant person.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we want to make sure that they have their benefits while they're pregnant, that they're able to continue to work just like anyone else, and that they can continue to support themselves.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks about CCHR's current disability caseload and trends. Kamuf Ward says she does not have total pending disability cases, and Rivera says the main trends are physically inaccessible housing and public accommodations and remote work requests in employment.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about current disability caseload and trends

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What is CCHR's current caseload on disability-related issues?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: concerns.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I don't have the total number of disability cases that are pending.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think we have, you know, how many are filed per year, but we'd have to go back and kind of run a more specific report to have how many cases that are before us involve disability.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then are you all tracking the...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Trends in areas, so elevator being one of them, the example around students with disabilities and school buses, like is that, do cases like that also come to your table?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What trends in issues are you all noticing?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You talked about housing discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Particularly in the housing context, and I would even say public accommodation space, the trend is physically inaccessible spaces predominantly.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: In the employment context, what we're seeing, especially since COVID back to work orders, individuals really relying on remote work as a reasonable accommodation option.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we're seeing definitely an increase in those as well.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks which cases take longest and raises the example of a ramp that took four years. Rivera says case length is fact-intensive and depends on modifications, city agencies, and number of respondents.
chapters.title: Hanif asks which cases take longest and about ramp delays

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Which cases are taking the longest?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Which kinds of cases are taking the longest to be resolved?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I don't think there's a particular type of case.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Again, it's very...

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And I hate to sound like a lawyer in this perspective, but it really is pretty fact intensive.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so it's going to depend on the complexity of the modification that's being requested.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: If we need to involve other city agencies such as DOB or Landmark Preservation Commission, how many respondents are involved and what the nature of the accommodation is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I mean, the example of the individual who was waiting for a ramp to get installed and dying in the process, I mean, that to me is avoidable, unavoidable circumstance

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: in terms of getting that ramp built.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Like, could you describe...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What the complexity we're dealing with, that a ramp took four years to get approved.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I know there's this challenge of needing to also work with the landlord or the building management in the process, and they have their own process.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand the trends because it seems to me that concerns regarding getting ramps built as an area of issue,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: that there's a systemic change that needs to get made so that a ramp isn't taking five years to get built.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That it is an area where we have...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Seen enough of these kinds of cases that it should only take six months, given we know from

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: start to end, what are the kinds of issues that will come up.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But so could you just describe a little bit more about, and I get the complexity being a part of each case, but there's absolutely no reason for a ramp taking, needing five years.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely, Chair Honey.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: You know, Project Equal Access is very successful, I would say, in ensuring and following through with ramp construction.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We often enter into settlement agreements prior to a complaint being filed that tries to closely track some of the issues that we know can come up with ramp installation, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Predominantly around a feasibility and getting appropriate architects through the door and beads dealing with

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: permit delays and those sorts of nuances and getting through with DOB.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: In the case that you're talking about in particular, Ray, I think the big issue is when we have

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: landlords that have become emboldened right now in this federal atmosphere and saying, we're not going to do this, we're not going to agree to do this,

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: or if they're raising undue burden defenses, particularly around finances, where we have to take a very analytical view of all of their resources, whether that's an individual LLC or business entity

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: or an individual person, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're requesting tax year.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: of tax records, bank account statements, rent rolls to see what really is the financial hardship here.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And ultimately, if we do have to go to litigation, we recognize that that is also a separate time-consuming process outside of our investigation efforts.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so trying to get that

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: through the door with OVE to a final decision in order can take time.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Although I recognize like we are moving quicker than probably a federally filed or state filed case.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We want to move these cases as quickly as possible in every instance.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether the ramp can be built while CCHR gathers documentation from a challenging landlord. Rivera says CCHR often must wait for the landlord and does not have authority to physically erect the ramp.
chapters.title: Hanif asks whether ramp construction can proceed during landlord delays

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So in the case that we're waiting for these DOB permits and there's

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: a challenging landlord, or like this process of needing to gather all of this material from the landlord.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are you saying that while that work is taking place, the ramp can't, that we can't have the ramp getting constructed?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Oftentimes that means we have to wait for the landlord to move forward with that process.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We don't have the authority to go in and physically erect that ramp ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I really wish we did.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether policy reform is needed so ramps can be built despite landlord delays. Nurse notes other agencies like HPD can make emergency repairs and bill owners, and Kamuf Ward says this is an area for interagency discussion.
chapters.title: Hanif and Nurse ask about policy reform and emergency repair authority

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: No, I totally understand that, that piece.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand through just our line of questioning here whether there's some policy reform that needs to get made while, like, sure, the landlord's going to be chattel.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: and we need to collect all of this documentation, but the ramp's gotta get built, no matter what.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Like, you're here, this is unlawful at this point, because we are an ADA accessible, and a city that follows

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: ADA accessibility no matter what.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So there has to be a cut through system.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'll go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Yeah, just to build on what you're saying, I know that other city agencies have the authority to go in and make emergency repairs, for example.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And in our district, we ask HPD to come in all the time when a landlord is being non-cooperative, and it is not a year-long process.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: You know, if something's happening, they will go in and do the emergency work and then bill the owner.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And I'm wondering what authority that could be extended here.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think that the difference is like being a service providing agency versus an anti-discrimination enforcement agency.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But I think, you know, this is probably an area of interagency discussion of kind of what are the tools to the extent that the undue hardship is financial, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Funds for building ramps.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But as the assistant commissioner was saying, you know, we can, we can order a settlement and we can find a violation, but in enforcing that is, is much more challenging than, you know, finding the violation.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: of the law.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think it's also different with, you know, buildings that are being built now that are, to your point, ADA accessible as a different ballgame than a building where it might be architecturally infeasible to build the ramp at the correct angle.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so then, you know, we will try for temporary solves or

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: where it's the only solution, you know, a ramp that can be installed and moved.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But yeah, I think this is an area for kind of ongoing conversation.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how long DOB typically takes to approve ramp permits. Rivera says prefabricated metal ramps can be done in weeks, while permanent fixtures can take six to nine months, and CCHR builds timelines into agreements.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about DOB permit timelines for ramps

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And we're spending too much time on ramps, but what is the typical length of time that DOB takes?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: To approve that request?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: for the permit to construct the ramp?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I couldn't say on average.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: What we've seen is ramps can take anywhere depending on how permanent of the structure.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: If they're installing a prefabricated metal ramp, and if that meets ADA guidelines for that building, that can definitely be done in a matter of weeks.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But then we've also had more permanent fixtures can take anywhere from six to nine months.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And again, we try to track those.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We ensure in our agreements that they follow specific timelines in refiling with DOB.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: If DOB comes back and says, hey, we need this revised or we need an additional document, creating affirmative obligations on those landlords that says you have to answer back to DOB within this certain time frame so the movement doesn't stop.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether businesses face the same process for ramps and accessibility accommodations. Rivera says yes, and Kamuf Ward notes public accommodations often involve both the store and building owner, adding more parties and cost questions.
chapters.title: Hanif asks whether business ramps follow the same process

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And is that the same for when a business needs to create a ramp or create accessibility accommodations as well?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yes, similar route for us.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the difference with stores, public accommodations, that it's often the store and the building owner.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So there's more players at the table, which again leads into the burden shifting of who's going to pay for it, what do the financials look like, but otherwise generally the same.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the city needs more reporting on public design and red tape around accessibility. She asks MOPD whether it has policy suggestions like enforceable deadlines or expedited review, and Morig says MOPD is building a policy team and everything is on the table.
chapters.title: Hanif calls for report on public design and asks MOPD for policy suggestions

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, and as I'm hearing you all just share more information, I mean,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I think even more important that our city have a report on this issue of public design and disability and these impacts and the complexity of public design as being

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: so incredibly red tape that it's so difficult when to all of us it feels like, oh, it's a ramp and this should happen much faster.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But I, yeah, I would really appreciate some more.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: or reporting on this so that there's more public awareness on these conditions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to come back to MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I know you mentioned that you're not necessarily providing recommendations to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: However,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Has there been any conversation on areas where, or internally, maybe not directly with CCHR, where you all

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: feel CCHR, that there should be changes to the human rights law for there to be faster and more meaningful relief for New Yorkers with disabilities?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Enforceable deadlines for accommodation cases as an example or should there should emergency cases such as tenants unable to enter or leave their homes

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: receive expedited review or interim relief should repeat accessibility violations carry higher or mandatory penalties are there

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: these kinds of maybe policy suggestions that you all are internally thinking about when it comes to cases like that are referred out to CCHR.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: This administration is really prioritizing disability communities

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: right to live a dignified life and have access to everything that they need, including physical accessibility and resources.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: Our vision is to move beyond just compliance and to just have, build an inclusive culture within the administration.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And so one of the first things that Commissioner Agarwal did in her new role is slowly build out a policy team.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And so this is something that we're actively working on and exploring.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: And we are, you know, everything's on the table for us.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We want to re-envision ways that the city could do better in serving people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We are, you know, we're in the early stages of that work.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We are collecting the data.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We are, you know, trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: We're constantly in the community.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: You know, the disabled community is a partner.

utterances.speaker: Belkis Morig
utterances.text: In the process and so this is certainly a priority that we're working towards and one of our, you know, one of the things that we want to prioritize.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks MOPD and passes questioning to Council Member Nurse for additional questions.
chapters.title: Hanif passes questioning to Nurse

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'll pass it to Council Member Nurse for additional questions.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how many disability cases are resolved by settlement versus administrative closure. Rivera says FY26 had 22 disability settlements and 59 administrative closures, and explains reasons like inability to locate complainants, withdrawal, or lack of public interest.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about settlements versus administrative closures

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, I want to just touch a little bit on resolution and timelines.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: For CCHR, when you have disability-related cases, can you talk about how many of those are resolved via settlement versus administrative closure?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So physical year 26, we settled 22 cases that had disability listed

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: as a protected class in the complaint, but could also have additional protected classes alleged in the complaint as well.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So that does include even ones that are just disability as well.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Compared to, I'm sorry, administrative closures you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Yeah, which ones were settlements versus administrative closure and what kind of circumstances would lead to an administrative closure versus another means of resolution?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So we had 59 cases that were administratively closed last fiscal year, fiscal year 26.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Administrative closures, the reasons are really outlined in our statute.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So they're really going to focus on we can have anything from we're unable to locate a complainant after multiple attempts.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We may need to close that matter.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: If a complaint is being withdrawn, they might have entered into private settlement or decided they wanted to file in a different forum.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So that's also an option in the administrative closure.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: reserves that individual's right to pursue that claim in another forum.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And then we have other instances where if it's not in the public interest to pursue that case, we see this a lot with small landlords and small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Complainants want to maintain good relationships with those owners, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: They're often living in the same building as them.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Or it can be something where we believe that there isn't sufficient resources to find a probable cause determination.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so I know historically we've really overutilized administrative closures in that instance.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we're really focusing on shifting gears and making sure that complainants have a real answer about one way or the another about the status of their complaint and why it may or may not reach probable cause determination.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks why fewer cases are settling. Rivera says settlements are difficult to trend and depend on respondent cooperation and meaningful outcomes, while Kamuf Ward says attorneys are balancing settlements with trials and complex cases.
chapters.title: Nurse asks why settlements have fallen

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And we saw that the settlements have fallen, the number of settlements have fallen.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Why do you think there are fewer cases settling?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Settlements are very difficult to trend, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: They're going to be, A, we're really relying on the cooperation of the respondents in those cases.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And we're also really focusing on what meaningful resolution and outcomes we can achieve for individuals, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Whether that's emotional distress damages, back rent, rent credits, modifications to their home, securing apartments.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And on the broader side, right, we want to make sure that we're really calling respondents in, as the Deputy Commissioner of MOPD mentioned, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We don't want to think just about what it means to comply.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: How do we make sure that landlords and employers and providers of public accommodations are really building in policies that make gender, or excuse me, make equity and justice, right,

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: the status quo in every situation and not just responsive and punitive.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think I'll just add to that.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I mean, I think we've talked already about the role of attorneys.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It's the same folks who are working on settling cases that are also taking cases to trial, which can be quite labor-intensive and where you have, again, complex cases and complex facts.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we're looking at kind of how to marshal our resources all the time in terms of bringing cases to trial and getting kind of big, big wins, like some of the cases we've talked about, versus settling cases.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think just adding to what the assistant commissioner said.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks for an update on the legal technology expert and case management consultant. Kamuf Ward says the legal technology director has onboarded and is working with the Office of Civil Rights Enforcement, but procurement is a long process.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about legal technology consultant and case management

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And then just back to the state comptroller.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I believe you all reported to him that you hired a consultant for case management and data retrieval.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I know we talked a little bit about this earlier on.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: There were plans to hire a legal technology expert.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Can you give us an update on where we're at with that?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yes, the legal technology director.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: is my next door neighbor at work.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So he has been on boarded and is working largely with the Office of Civil Rights Enforcement, but really with all the teams in the agency

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: to make sure that any new system that we procure is, you know,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: best in class for our needs.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But as you probably also know, procurement is a long-term game.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's a fun process.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks about CCHR testing numbers and what enforcement followed. Rivera says CCHR has about three part-time testers and a supervisor, and disability testing dipped while salary transparency and fair chance housing testing grew.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about testing and commission-initiated enforcement

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, I want to just touch on testing and commission-initiated enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We've talked about testing quite a lot this year, so I'm not going to go too hard onto it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: In the FY26 report, CCHR's tests included 197 disability claims in public accommodations, 59 in housing and none in employment, down from 390 disability claims in FY25.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: What did those tests find and what enforcement followed?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So the test results, we'd have to pull specifics on each jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I would be happy to follow up with that.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
