utterances.text: But what we are able to do with our small testing team right now, we have about, I believe, three part-time testers and a direct full-time supervisor.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: They are testing across all jurisdictions, right, and across all protected classes.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so while there has been a dip in disability-focused testing, that's been in large part because of other protected classes that we've really been responsive to, particularly around salary transparency.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Fair chance housing as well has been a really big focus as we are trying to get individuals to report criminal history violations in housing applications, which we're also seeing as an overlap, again, with other protected classes as well.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how CCHR decides where to spend testing resources and whether it considers medical offices, ride hail apps, or co-op boards. Rivera says testing is dictated by public complaints, anonymous tips, and potential broad impact.
chapters.title: Nurse asks how CCHR decides testing priorities

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And then just how do you all decide each year where you want to spend your time and resources testing?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: For example, have you considered medical offices, ride shares, ride hail, apps, co-ops, and condo boards?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: How are you all making those determinations each year?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Testing is really going to be dictated by what we're hearing from the public.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: the types of complaints we're getting, you know, the anonymous tips that we receive, we will review those tips and see what's feasible for testing.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And if we think testing is of respondents of a certain size and stature that are going to have a broader impact, right, on the public.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So we want to be testing those large agencies and those large providers of public spaces, which is why the Barnes and Nobles Commission Initiative is so big.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And why are you all not testing employers on accommodation and hiring?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: For employment in particular, because of the nuances that go into job duty review and the amount of investigative work that does have to

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: be fronted a little bit, it's really difficult to do testing and employment in particular, or even reasonable accommodation investigations for pre-complaint postures.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Many of those cases, while we are expanding our pre-complaint interventions for employment in particular, those are often moving to complaint filings because of the depth of investigative work that we anticipate will go into those cases, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Many employers have some form of internal EEO process, whether it's just a single person or a large unit.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so that really is our opportunity, A, to make sure that businesses and employers do have a robust.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: EEO process that is taking into consideration every person's needs.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And if they're not, we're able to say, hey, these are the broader policy implications that need to happen so that it impacts every worker in that space.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks why disability testing fell by a third while arrest record, credit history, and salary history testing grew. Rivera says the testing team is small and resources also support public-initiated complaints and strategic enforcement.
chapters.title: Nurse asks why disability testing fell while other tests grew

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I'd be curious.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I mean, because you're talking about the size of employers that might have that type of staffing or that size of an organization where you might have an EEO or an HR kind of department,

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: but maybe where small businesses or two to three people working in a place might be needed.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: A question on why did disability testing fall by a third while tests on arrest record, credit history, and salary history each grew by half?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: For testing in particular, thank you, Chair Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: For testing in particular, we are, again, a very small team.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Some of those resources are also to support public-initiated complaints brought by members of the public, where we're trying to see if we can substantiate further their claims, and so that may divert resources as well.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We do have our new strategic enforcement unit that is also focusing on those broader impact cases and are starting to really rely on our testing team as well.

chapters.summary: Nurse says it sounds like CCHR needs more resources, and Rivera says they can go further faster with more. Nurse notes the Council advocated for CCHR funding and ends her questions.
chapters.title: Nurse says CCHR needs more resources and ends questions

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So it sounds like you guys need more resources.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We can go further with more faster.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Well, we did advocate for you all this year.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, that's the end of my questions, I think.

chapters.summary: Hanif passes questioning to Council Member Rita Joseph and says she will return with a few more questions.
chapters.title: Hanif passes questioning to Council Member Joseph

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to pass it to Councilmember Joseph, and then I'll come back to a few more questions.

chapters.summary: Joseph describes elevator outages in her district and asks what changes CCHR made after accepting the comptroller's recommendations. Kamuf Ward says CCHR renamed its enforcement office, moved staff into enforcement, and created dedicated training and community partnerships teams.
chapters.title: Joseph asks what changed after comptroller recommendations

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Some of the questions around elevators has been one of the biggest things in my district, where folks have to remain in rehabilitation centers because they cannot come home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And my older adults are stuck in the apartments, can't make it to their doctor's appointments, or go out to do regular food shopping, and community members have to step in.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I think on our side, we need to do better.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Landlords have to also step up and do their part, but I think we need to do better.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want to go back to the controllers.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Comptroller's recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So you accepted the audit's recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And what has changed?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The recommendations they gave you, what changes have you made?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I think, you know, as part of this administration and under Commissioner Clark, we have really reimagined what it means to be doing civil rights enforcement, right?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I think the lead of that was changing the name of our team from Law Enforcement Bureau to Office of Civil Rights Enforcement so people know what we do.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It's clear on its face, but it's really moving staff into the enforcement team and moving staff with cultural competency, language ability into roles on the enforcement team.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we have shifted people from, you know, doing some forms of outreach and engagement to that outreach being more connected to the enforcement side.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I'd say that's the biggest shift is marshalling our number one resource, our people that work for us and come to work every day because they care about civil rights in New York City, and really focusing on case times.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We've also now, as a result of that reorg, have a kind of dedicated team focused on trainings, where it used to be that that was part of people's jobs.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And we have a community partnerships team, which is really serving as the focal point for nonprofit and in.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: interagency partnerships.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how accessible CCHR is for ASL, plain language, Braille, video, and screen readers, and for disabled New Yorkers who do not speak English. Rivera says CCHR has screen reader services, ASL interpreters, large print, Braille, multiple languages, and a vendor for translation.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about accessibility of CCHR services and languages

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how accessible are you in terms, both of you, how accessible are you and how can not someone file a complaint through, can they use ASL, plain language, Braille by video?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is the online portal screen reader accessible as well?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I will say I am personally very accessible, as well as my team.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I'm very honored to say to anyone who asks us, if you're reaching out to the commission, you're going to hear back from somebody, and you're going to get a live person.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: In terms of accessibility in particular, we do have screen reader services.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We have ASL interpreters.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We may not always have them on site.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So if we do have someone who walks into our office, we are an open office.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Individuals can come in without an appointment.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We will try to secure an ASL interpreter for them.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: If not, we'll schedule an appointment for them within days so that they can come back and get exactly what they need.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Many of our materials are available in large print, as well as Braille and in multiple languages.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That was going to be my next follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What about disabled New Yorkers who don't speak English?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What languages do you provide?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And if it's not on site, do you outsource that?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We do have a vendor that services us.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I'm just thinking about a case that I've been working with our director of InfoLine, where the individual...

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: is deaf and blind, but only speaks Arabic.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so really figuring out what's the best and most efficient way to communicate with that individual.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And we've scheduled them up with an appointment while we secure ASL interpretation to do that double translation for us.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether CCHR is seeing more disability cases as federal civil rights offices scale back. Rivera says complaints and inquiries have increased, and explains remedies against city agencies include policy changes, trainings, and long-term monitoring.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about increase in disability cases and city agency remedies

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is CCHR seeing more disability cases as federal civil rights offices scale back on these rights?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are you seeing an increase in numbers?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: There is an increase in the number of complaints filed and the inquiries that we're seeing for sure, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Whether it's a direct correlation, I think we can say affirmatively, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Like there is something happening there and people are choosing to come to us now that their identities and their protected classes are under attack at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And when CCHR find a city agency at fault, what remedy applies and who makes sure they are carried out?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah, when another one get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So we do have authority over our sibling agencies.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: While we may not seek civil penalties per se, right, we're often looking again for that affirmative relief that ingrains, right, equity and justice in their policies.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: More significantly, we require in trainings, many times we are doing the trainings ourselves to make sure the training is adequate and appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're requiring that individual policies are revamped and we will approve.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Those policies have to come to us for approval before they're able to implement them.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And in significant cases, we can require long-term monitoring to make sure that compliance is happening year after year.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many remote accommodation complaints CCHR receives and whether it has seen AI hiring tool complaints. Rivera says she does not have remote work numbers but it is a trend, and Kamuf Ward says CCHR works with DCWP on the bias audit law but has not had disability-focused AI complaints.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about remote accommodation complaints and AI hiring tools

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Chair, can I ask one more question?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So how many remote accommodation complaints come in, including city employees?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you have numbers?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I don't have those particular numbers.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I believe we can try to pull them manually.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But it is, as I mentioned earlier, it is the trend that we're seeing in employment cases for remote work in particular, either full or partial.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I'm just going to close this one out.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Has CCHR received disability complaints involving AI hiring tool?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Does it court?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: with DCWP, which enforces the city automated hiring law.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How is that working together?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, so we worked very closely with DCWP on kind of the guidelines for the bias audit law, which I remember part of the number, the intro or the actual one.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But we have, to my knowledge, we have not had disability-focused complaints related to AI specifically, though there could be some of the hiring or employment cases involve automated decision-making technology.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But we work very closely with DCWP both on kind of outreach and policy as well as on enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Enforcement and training as well as you say you do training into interagencies, correct?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much, chairs.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks about cases from city agency employees on remote work access. Rivera says she will circle back and mentions settlements with NYC Transit employees, and Kamuf Ward explains city employees first go through agency EEO processes and accommodations are job-specific.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about city employee remote work cases and policy

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit more about the cases coming from city agency employees on remote work access?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: For those, I can't think of off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: It's something that we may need to circle back on, Chair Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But thinking about just sibling agency cases overall, right, we are often pursuing and settling matters,

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: particularly in the employment field, right?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We've had several settlements with New York City Transit employees in the subway systems.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We've also recently had a settlement in the public accommodation space as New York City Transit, as you mentioned in your opening, where we were able to really secure a

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: meaningful financial compensation for those individuals that were refused entry on buses because of their reliance on a service animal.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But then also reaching postings really across all five boroughs in bus depots and in the buses themselves so that individuals know, right, you have a right to enter this bus with your service animal.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And here are the appropriate questions that any bus operator should be able to ask and receive answers for.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I'll just say for city employees, right, city agencies have their EEO officer, which is the first stop,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: and then there can be an internal appeal, or if your reasonable accommodation request is denied, that could come to CCHR or go to the EEOC or the state division.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So there's a kind of multiplicity of venues where those cases might end up.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm very.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: curious about remote work access being denied, given there was a huge fight by city employees to get a more clarified policy on the ability to work remote.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So we can certainly circle back, but what's the current policy on remote work access?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I think, I mean, the city, like everyone else under the city human rights law, right, is if someone requests an accommodation,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: again, the first stop is the EEO officer is going to look at the particular position, what the individual's needs and limitations are, and then discuss what are feasible, you know, accommodations.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And that, you know, is...

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Also lives alongside the collective bargaining agreements and all of the other rules, but it's going to be very, again, as the assistant commissioner was saying, it's very job specific because if you have a frontline,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: you know, public facing position, it's different than if you are someone who's doing something where you're not interacting with the public.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many complaints CCHR has received about inaccessible sidewalks, blocked curb cuts, or public right-of-way barriers. Kamuf Ward says CCHR does not have that number and will circle back, and says CCHR can provide some breakdowns of reasonable accommodation versus other claims.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about curb cut complaints and case breakdowns

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then a point that was

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: made a comment that was made earlier about curb cuts I wanted to come back to because curb cuts certainly are an issue of disability and discrimination and thank God for disability advocates for fighting for curb cuts.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How many complaints has CCHR received regarding inaccessible

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: sidewalks, blocked curb cuts, or other barriers in the public.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Right of way.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I don't think we don't have that number with us today.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think often when a complaint is coming to us, like it could be because a street is blocked for something like open, you know, open streets where people can't get into their houses.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But I'm not familiar with how many curb cut cases have come to us.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I don't know if you know anecdotally.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we'd have to circle back to see if we have that data.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you all, there are buckets of issue areas.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That you're going to be able to share with us on what kinds of cases are being handled at the moment, whether it be about...

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: You mean within the disability space?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yes, within the disability space.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll be able to do some breakdowns of reasonable accommodations versus other claims at a certain level of granularity our system can't report out, or we'd have to run a manual tabulation of all of the cases.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So we'll circle back.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So we will certainly follow up again.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what enforcement action CCHR takes when a landlord, employer, or business refuses a reasonable accommodation. Rivera says those cases move to probable cause and litigation at OATH, and repeat offenders face no pre-complaint intervention, higher civil penalties, and monitoring.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about enforcement when accommodations are refused and repeat offenders

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: When CCHR determines that an accommodation is reasonable, but a landlord, employer, or business refuses to provide it, what enforcement action do you all take?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Yes, those are absolutely the cases that are moving forward, likely with probable cause determinations that then we have to do litigation at oath for a decision and order.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how does CCHR handle repeat offenders of disability-based discrimination, like the Transit Authority in two separate disability settlements in the 2026 annual report,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: one over bus riders with service animals and one over an employee's use of sick leave?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is it treated as a repeat?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are they being treated as a repeat offender?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And does that affect penalties or enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: When we, depending on the violation type and the number of instances, they're absolutely considered a repeat offender.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Particularly for repeat offenders, we're often, A, we will eliminate any sort of pre-complaint interventions with them.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We don't want them to think that, oh, if you're going to agree to a pre-complaint intervention, that this is just going to go away for you.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Those are the instances where we are seeking significant civil penalties, where we're going to constantly increase the imposition of those numbers until we reach the maximum, which is only set at $250,000 right now.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And that is unfortunately the cap that we have to work with in each violation.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Again, affirmative relief is going to be a big component as well in those sorts of settlements or decisions where we're seeking significant internal change.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: and monitoring of those offenders.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether there is a public list of worst disability discrimination offenders. Kamuf Ward says the comptroller has an employee dashboard and CCHR is advocating to increase statutory maximum civil penalties because current caps may not deter.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about public list of worst offenders and penalties

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And we don't have a public list like we do for the worst landlord watch list for agencies or companies, businesses that are the worst of the worst when it comes to...

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Actually, this is not a CCHR initiative.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: The Comptroller does have an employee dashboard.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It looks at a whole host of different cases.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so there is something that exists in that arena.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But I wanted to just underscore, and I think we've talked a little bit with the Civil and Human Rights Committee about the kind of the civil penalties as

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: maybe not serving the same deterrent effect that they served when they were updated in 2005.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so there's been kind of an affirmative push by CCHR, and we're in conversation, I think, with you all as partners, but with City Hall as well, about increasing the statutory maximum of civil penalties so that they can

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: truly serve a deterrent effect and to allow there to be discretion that matches the wide variety of cases that we see.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We don't have a per violation statute.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We look at an array of factors for civil penalties, and I think that's an area of collaboration.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how CCHR sets penalties and how often it pursues the maximum. Rivera says factors include public impact, size and sophistication of the bad actor, cooperation, and egregiousness, and explains the normal cap is $125,000 and maximum is $250,000 for willful and egregious violations.
chapters.title: Hanif asks how CCHR sets penalties and about statutory maximum

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So would you be able to share how you're setting the penalties?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: So how penalties are set is really determined and laid out by several factors in our case law.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: That can include the public impact.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We believe it's going to impact more individuals.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We're going to increase civil penalties.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: The size and sophistication of the bad actor is going to play a big part as well.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We look at their willingness and cooperation during our investigation, if it is something that we can quickly resolve.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And also, honestly, the egregiousness of the incident is going to play a large factor as well.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And you said that the statutory maximum is $200,000?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: $250,000 if we can demonstrate that the violation was willful and egregious.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: The normal cap is about $125,000.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I was going to mention that the 2026 report...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Penalties range from none to $110,000.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How often are you pursuing the statutory maximum?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Because we do want it to be a true deterrent effect, you know, we're really seeking maximum penalties for those particularly egregious cases and repeat offenders.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: It is a tool that, of course, we're going to try and utilize in settlement negotiations, and so we might not necessarily start off with that number.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But if we are moving to trial, we know that a case is particularly egregious and a respondent has the resources and it's going to make the impact that we think it is, we're going to advocate and argue for the most penalties possible.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how CCHR ensures settlements produce lasting accessibility improvements and who monitors compliance. Rivera says CCHR designated a monitoring clerk and attorneys supervise compliance, with deadlines for policies, training, and postings.
chapters.title: Hanif asks how CCHR monitors lasting accessibility improvements

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How are you all ensuring that settlements produce lasting accessibility improvements and who's monitoring the compliance?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What's the frequency?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We are directly monitoring compliance.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We do, in part of our reorg, we've designated a monitoring clerk who is responsible for ensuring that actors are complying either with the decision in order or in the settlement terms and conditions.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so when they do not comply in the time frame, that monitoring clerk is quickly notifying the appropriate attorney or supervisors.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: But really it is on us to ensure that, A, policies are being changed, training is being completed, postings are going up for reasonable accommodations.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We do prioritize those being finished, and so we may set quicker turnaround times and deadlines for those in particular.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so the attorney who settled the matter may often personally supervise and ensure that that accommodation is followed through.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And this monitoring clerk, is this role, you said this is new?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How recent?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: The role itself is new.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: It is a part, it was a current staff member that we've designated.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so this is a new role and responsibility for them.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Before the reorganization, it was on each individual attorney who settled the case to also monitor compliance.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I will just say we also work with the law department on the enforcement side, especially where there's, you know, finances involved.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So it's we have our attorneys who are doing their best to hold people accountable, but it often also requires other follow up outside of CCHR.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many settlements are under active monitoring and how many New Yorkers received requested accommodations. Rivera says she will follow up on monitoring numbers, and Kamuf Ward says CCHR tracks whether matters resolved but not always the exact final accommodation.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about active monitoring and accommodation outcomes

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How many settlements are currently under active monitoring?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I would be happy to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I'm not sure off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And this is something that would be under the purview of the monitoring clerk to know?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And can CCHR share how many New Yorkers with disabilities received the accommodation they requested?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In FY26?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think we won't have that data because it's not always the accommodation that someone that's requested.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We are not tracking necessarily what the end accommodation is in all instances, but we are

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: tracking the kind of the cooperative dialogue, whether it was engaged, what the kind of violations of the law are, and it is part of the reasonable accommodation process that there may be a back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So the thing, even if someone succeeds at the reasonable accommodation claim, it might not be the original thing they requested.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It might be an alternative accommodation.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And do you have that data to share?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I think we can share information on how many cases involved reasonable accommodations.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I don't know we will be able to pull exactly that data.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm trying to understand from...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Someone who filed a complaint about, let's say, a ramp and by

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: the end of the year, some solution did happen.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And that solution,

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Yeah, so we can track the matter resolved, right?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Accommodation granted or resolved in favor of the individual.

chapters.summary: Hanif notes the FY26 MMR credits Project Equal Access with a 70 percent rise in accessibility modifications. Rivera says the expansion was one additional full-time staff member, bringing the team to three.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about Project Equal Access expansion

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The fiscal 2026 MMR credits expanded project equal access capacity for a 70% rise in accessibility modifications from 61 to 104.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What did the expansion consist of, and is that funding and staffing permanent?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: The big change was that we got an additional staff member for Project Equal Access.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: I previously only had two members holding down the fort.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And now we have another full-time staff member that was pulled in from another unit.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks who monitors policy changes or training when CCHR settles with a city agency and whether MOPD plays a role. Rivera says CCHR monitors those settlements, and Kamuf Ward says city employee accommodation denials first go through agency EEO processes and DCAS holds EEO information.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about city agency settlements and employee coordination

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Joseph asked some questions about city agencies as respondents.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: When CCHR settles a disability case against a city agency, who monitors the policy changes or training the settlement requires?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And does MOPD play a role in that?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We still do all the monitoring in those cases as well from policy revisions, again, monitoring any training requirements.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: We are often requiring that staff members involved or the agency, anyone that is going to have that public contact is doing our trainings.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Rivera
utterances.text: And so we want to make sure that they're getting the right training every time.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: When a city employee is denied reasonable accommodation, how do CCHR, DCAS, and agency EEO offices coordinate?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how are employees being informed of their rights to file directly with CCHR?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we would only hear a city agency denial of a reasonable accommodation case if someone, after they go through the internal process at their agency, decides to file with us.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we don't have general information.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: DCAS is the one that holds the information about what is the activity for the EEO officers at any...

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: given agency, we're only involved if someone files a discrimination claim at CCHR.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what education or training the city provides about service animal access and how it compares to Intro 1107. Kamuf Ward describes Human Rights Law 101, disability protections trainings, settlement-required trainings, and posters from the NYC Transit case and MOPD.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about service animal education and training

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, that's good to know.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: On my bill, I know the administration shows support.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What education or training does the city currently provide to businesses about service animal access?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how does that compare with what this bill would require?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So I can speak to CCHR, and I think MOPD has trainings as well that can be spoken to.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So we have Human Rights Law 101.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It's our kind of most prevalent training that we offered, I think, 420 times last year, reaching about 20,000 people.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: That includes businesses.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It includes small businesses.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We participate with SBS and a number of small business activities.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: It includes city agencies and nonprofits as well.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So that's our Human Rights Law 101.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: We also have a specific training on disability protections in housing and public accommodations that was offered several hundred times last year and reached about

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: 10,000 people.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: As the assistant commissioner mentioned, trainings are ordered as part of our settlements.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So if you are responding in a case, you are going to be hearing from us on what the law requires.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: But also there's many, many.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: kind of requests every week to our trainings team to come and affirmatively provide education and outreach.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I'm just going to lift up again some of the cases that we've talked about today because the NYC transit case, one of the elements of that case is that buses across the five boroughs now have to post a

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: service animals are allowed on public transportation poster.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And so that is a way to inform New Yorkers about their rights.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: In the housing case that we mentioned, the Tabri decision and order, the landlord has been required to post reasonable accommodation protections in the building, again, to raise awareness in particular places where we think discrimination might be happening

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: about what people's rights are.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And CCHR and MOPD also have a service animal and public accommodations poster that is already available.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: I will say there's other sibling agencies who also have a role, I think, in this particular bill because it touches on so many areas of public accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: So there's a number of codes that are kind of outside of the discrimination space that are at play.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I know there's a mayor's office of animal welfare who has done a number of educational materials and has a website that touches upon a number of the pieces of this bill.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: And I think that's part of the reason that we're still reviewing with law and sibling agencies to identify.

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: What is duplicative and where this

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: would most effectively live.

chapters.summary: Hanif says those are all the questions and asks if the administration wants to share anything before public testimony. Kamuf Ward thanks the Council for the hearing and looks forward to continuing to work together.
chapters.title: Hanif asks if witnesses have anything to add before public testimony

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That's very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Those are all the questions we have.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is there anything you'd like to share before we move to public testimony?

utterances.speaker: JoAnn Kamuf Ward
utterances.text: No, just I think thank you for your time and for this hearing topic and look forward to continuing to work together.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks the witnesses and announces a five-minute break before returning to public testimony.
chapters.title: Hanif announces five-minute break before public testimony

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif

chapters.summary: Hanif moves to public testimony and reminds attendees this is a government proceeding requiring decorum. She explains that witnesses get four minutes, written testimony can be submitted to the sergeant at arms or by email within 72 hours, and audio/video recordings are not accepted.
chapters.title: Hanif opens public testimony and explains rules

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We will now move to...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please take a seat, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the sergeant at arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If you wish to speak today, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have four minutes to speak on today's oversight topic.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If you have a written statement,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Will not be accepted.
