chapters.summary: Clement So, executive director of the Metropolitan Asian Deaf Association, says CCHR lacks direct ASL video intake and centralized data on accessibility violations experienced by deaf residents. He says without direct video intake and systematic data collection, CCHR cannot measure disability discrimination or direct enforcement effectively.
chapters.title: Clement So testifies on CCHR data collection and ASL video intake

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Good morning, chair members of this council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: My name is Clement So, executive director of the Metropolitan Asian Deaf Association, or MADA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: We're advocates for communication access and civil rights for deaf, hard of hearing, and deafblind New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: I am here today to address a few critical points regarding CCHR's enforcement role in key pending legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: One, strengthening CCHR's data collection and direct accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: While CCHR plays a vital role in investigating discrimination, critical operation gaps hamper its ability to protect deaf New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: There's no direct ASL video at the intake line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: CCHR currently lacks a dedicated directly accessible video communication line, such as a direct video phone channel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Deaf and ASL signing residents face immediate language and technical barriers when attempting to file complaints or report discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Severe data collection deficit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: CCHR currently maintains no active metrics or centralized reporting frameworks tracking accessibility violations experienced by deaf residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: CCHR lacks comprehensive information on these trends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Without direct video intake and systematic data collection, CCHR cannot accurately measure the scope of disability discrimination in NYC or direct its enforcement effectively.

chapters.summary: So says MADA strongly supports Intro 1107 and urges plain language education, model language, and publication in citywide languages and accessible formats. He also supports the resolution calling on the Senate to ratify the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
chapters.title: Clement So supports Intro 1107 and UNCRPD resolution

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Strong support for intro T2026-2657.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Service Animal Guidance and Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Mata strongly supports Intro T2026-2657.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Deaf and blind handlers continuously face illegal denial of entry, harassment, and confusion from business owners who do not understand service animal rights under the NYC Human Rights Law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: We urge the Council to mandate plain language education pamphlets, standardized model language, and publication in all designated citywide languages and accessible formats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Strong support for Resolution T-2026-2637, UNCRPD ratification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: MADA enthusiastically supports Resolution T-2026-2637, calling for the Senate to approve and the President to ratify the UN Convention of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Disability rights are international human rights, and ratifying the CRPD reinforces global standards for sign language recognition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: full societal inclusions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: In conclusion, to truly protect deaf New Yorkers, CCHR must modernize its intake infrastructure with direct video communication lines and actively gather on disability trends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and your leadership and for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Hanif moves to Monique Bourne, whose statement is read by an interpreter. Bourne says she reported disability-related barriers involving HRA and APS to CCHR in September 2025 but received no explained assessment or corrective intervention.
chapters.title: Monique Bourne testifies on CCHR, HRA, and APS discrimination

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Clement, and thank you to our interpreter who's accompanying you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We'll go to Zoom to hear from Monique Bourne.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is Morinike on?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And do you mind telling me your name to the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm asking the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Brandon K.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Boyce.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Brandon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clement So
utterances.text: I am reading a statement by Morinike Arborn, who has requested an accommodation to have her testimony presented on her behalf.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My contribution to this meeting regarding civil rights and human rights is that I do not feel my civil rights or liberties have been recognized and respected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I feel I have been repeatedly denied meaningful due process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: On September 28, 2025, I reported disability-related barriers involving HRA and APS to the City Commission on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I described being ignored or denied accommodations, inaccessible application and appeal procedures, and the absence of individualized consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I followed up with support records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: And expressly requested investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: The Commission's Law Enforcement Bureau acknowledged my report and promised a telephone follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: On October 15th, it replied on a landlord correspondence thread that the situation did not appear covered by the NYC Human Rights Law and directed me

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: to telephone intake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: That response did not explain how it assessed my actual disability access allegations, what recordings it considered, and whether it was disposing of my earlier report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I still have no explained assessment or corrective intervention that opened the assistance process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I understand the commission does not award rental subsidies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I asked it to address discrimination in access to city services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: HRA denied an application I had never been allowed to complete or review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My city FEPS appeal waited a year for a scheduled hearing, then faced missing records and later proceeded without my participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Where was the meaningful review while my home remained at risk?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I have housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I need it preserved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: CityFEP stands for City Fighting Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: But where is the city fighting homelessness in my household?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: In my experience, the opposite is happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My efforts to stabilize this home meets resistance, and the doors to the assistance program, to the assistance process, remains shut as homelessness encroaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I have not seen action with the urgency needed to stop it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My household should have been a straightforward housing preservation case if stabilization is a priority and its pathways are operational.

chapters.summary: Bourne describes a disability set-aside apartment, a rent freeze, and landlord support for CityFEP, but says she faces a third non-payment proceeding. She asks the Council to scrutinize why preserving an existing home is so difficult and why access is concentrated after homelessness occurs.
chapters.title: Monique Bourne details housing preservation case and asks for scrutiny

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My mother and I obtained this disability set aside apartment through Housing Connect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: It is rent stabilized and protected by low income housing tax credit affordability restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My lease is renewed through May 2027.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Dree freezes my rent at $1,309 through May 31st, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My landlord provided a letter of support and agreed to accept city FEPS and cooperate with the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: After my mother died, the income supporting our rent disappeared.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: And the home did not become unsuitable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My tenancy remains overwhelmingly viable if the needed arrears assistance and ongoing rent support become accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Yet instead of stabilization, I have encountered resistance while the tenancy deteriorates and hangs in the balance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I sought help before housing court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I have supplied records, pursued appeals, and requested accommodations, but I now face a third non-payment proceeding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: My tendency is battered, just as I am battered, but we are still here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Why did my tendency and I have to endure all of this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: If there are several pathways for people with disabilities and special needs, why have I faced

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: repeated housing court proceedings despite my landlord support, my renewed lease, my DRE protection, and my repeated efforts to meet the requirements communicated to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I live with a disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Homebase requires APS approval, but APS denied services, citing my efforts to seek help for myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Those efforts have come at a serious cost to my health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I am struggling to keep my home, and I still need assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Repeated requests and paperwork cannot replace the income we've lost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: On January 27, 2025, Commissioner Parks said there was absolutely exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: On June 4, 2026, Scott French described one-shot deals as a first resource, case-by-case consideration, and several pathways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Brandon, can you wrap up the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: And we are going to be reviewing all of the testimonies submitted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: But we will be moving on to our next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Why is access so concentrated after homelessness has occurred?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: Why is preserving an existing home so difficult?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monique Bourne
utterances.text: I ask the council to scrutinize that imbalance and the barriers to prevention.

chapters.summary: Jean Ryan, president of Disabled in Action, says a Bay Ridge grocery store locked a gate during business hours, blocking wheelchair and walker users. She says CCHR took her case almost four years ago but nothing has legally stopped the store, and her emails to the commissioner have gone unanswered.
chapters.title: Jean Ryan testifies on locked grocery gate and CCHR delay

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Monique.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We're moving on to Jean Ryan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Jean Ryan, wheelchair user and president of Disabled in Action in Metropolitan New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Are you going to the grocery store today after work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: I bet you know that you can go right in and you won't be locked out by a gate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: 25 and 30 years ago, that used to be a common occurrence for wheelchair users, that we'd be locked out and upright people could get into grocery stores with no problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Then the NYC Human Rights Commission helped us get our civil rights and have access to grocery stores without the gates being locked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Now it's happening again in some stores, and we can forget about getting any help from the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Four years ago, next month, so it's like in two weeks, it's going to be four years, a grocery store in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn Harvest Market, started locking a gate during business hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: That kept out wheelchair and walker users, people who use strollers, and people with their own large shopping carts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Upright people could walk right in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Sometimes I was able to gain access by waiting outside and asking a stranger to ask them to come out and unlock the gate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: But walking people didn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: They could walk right in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: I talked with the manager and he didn't

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: I complained to the Human Rights Commission, and they took my case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: But in almost four years, nothing has happened on their end to legally stop Brooklyn Harvest Market.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Now the gate is unlocked, but there is nothing preventing them from locking the gate whenever they want.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And recently, another grocery store in Bay Ridge had a locked gate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: For months, my case has not been assigned to anyone, and my emails to the commissioner have gone unanswered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: I emailed her six weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: go on September 4th and have not gotten an answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: I asked Moped to intervene and nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: They did try.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Why is nothing happening?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Why is this case dragging on for four years?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Everyone has the right to shop in a grocery store.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: The Human Rights Commission has become irrelevant to most people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: They aren't there for us to protect our rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: We don't even think of them as a resource.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: That needs to change.

chapters.summary: Ryan describes an Uber case brought by several people with disabilities that was taken individually and eventually discontinued with a $1,000 offer. She says she wanted access, not money, and questions why CCHR is not helping people with disabilities enforce their civil rights.
chapters.title: Jean Ryan testifies on Uber case and access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Also, I'd like to quickly mention an Uber case that six or seven of us brought as a group, but they took us individually

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: because Uber does not give the same service, same equal treatment to people with disabilities as it does to people without disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And every year somebody would call from the Human Rights Commission and say, are you still interested in keeping the case?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And he'd say, okay, bye.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And call me in another year and ask me the same question until one year he said, well, Uber will give you $1,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: We're discontinuing the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Why are you discontinuing the case?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: He wouldn't say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: But do you want the $1,000 or not?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: I said, no, I want access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: That's what we sue for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: That's what the complaint was about, was access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: We have to wait.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: way longer than somebody else does who doesn't use a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And, you know, so they closed the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: None of us knew why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: They didn't say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: So why would we come to the, I mean, it's supposed to be a resource, but why would we go to the CCHR if they're not going to help us get our rights, our civil rights?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Michael Ring, vice president of Disabled in Action, says service animals are life-changing and not pets. He supports the city's educational campaign on service animals and describes confusion among poll workers about service animals versus pets.
chapters.title: Michael Ring supports service animal education campaign

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Michael Ring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: If anyone needs a verbal description of my appearance, I'm a 63-year-old white guy who needs a shave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And I'm wearing a green hat that says Disabled in Action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I happen to be the vice president.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I'm wearing a hoodie that says I ran a marathon because I'm complicated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I wanted to talk about the proposals to give more information about service animals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And a little background about myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I've never been a fan of pets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: My kids hate me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: You can all pile on, but it's just not a thing for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: But I acquired a disability 12 and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And since then, I hang around with a lot of people with various disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I have volunteered in hospitals, and I've seen service animals are life-extending, life-saving, life-changing things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: People could...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: They are as important as wheelchairs and ramps and elevators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: They're not pets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Pets are luxuries, and people need service animals to get out of their house, to go to work, to live their lives, to be alive, not just to live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: There's, and then I'm looking at these posters on the buses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I take the bus a lot now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: People read the posters and go, oh, there's a difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: So I'm so excited that the city wants to move forward and have an educational campaign because I'm also a poll worker and I'm a coordinator and I get conflicting information on how to deal with pets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Some of the instructors say if someone wants to walk in with a parrot on their shoulder, don't say anything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Others understand the difference between a service animal and a pet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Codifying this and educating our population would make it much safer for people to have their service animals because often pets don't interact well with service animals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And I just wanted to say how happy I was that this is moving forward and any way that Disabled in Action could support this, we're all in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And thanks for your time.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Who walked into the pool with a parrot?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: No, no, an instructor said that would be okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, that's good to know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And I've been in my polling place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Two dogs had a fight, and a civilian, someone who didn't bring the dog, was knocked down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And neither of those dogs was a service animal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: But our coordinator that day said, don't tell anyone not to come in.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thanks for sharing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Thanks.

chapters.summary: Masa Mehta, representing the National Federation of the Blind of New York, says she has been denied entry and refused service at restaurants, retail stores, and public agencies because businesses do not know service animal rules. She supports Intro 1107 and says information must be accessible and service animal handlers must be involved in reviewing materials.
chapters.title: Masa Mehta testifies on service animal denials and Intro 1107

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We'll pass it now to Mossa Miata.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: My name is Masa Mehta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I am representing the National Federation of the Blind of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I am a service animal handler myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I have my guide dog with me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: She is not a parrot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: And I wanted to speak a little bit in support of the educational campaign and the guidance and information for service animal handlers and businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I myself have been denied entry and refused service from quite a few places, unfortunately, retail establishments, restaurants, even public agencies, because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: either businesses don't know the difference between an emotional support animal and a service animal, or they don't know the ADA or the provisions or the NYC human rights law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Both of these are pretty big problems to not know about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: And it's really tough because it's kind of this idea of a thousand paper cuts, you know, like this takes a huge toll on my community because essentially we're being shut out of accessing areas of public life that our fellow New Yorkers have access to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: And so this bill really aims to provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: clear information so that businesses can take advantage of our patronage, but we can also take advantage of their services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I also wanted to talk about the fact that I believe that businesses are not intentionally trying to break the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I think that in most cases, they just don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: And the city can do a huge service to this by modeling clear standards, providing these service animal welcome signs, and even, you know, thinking about how accessibility plays in as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Someone from the MOPD had mentioned these signs in bus stops saying that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Everyone has the right to enter with a service animal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: So it kind of goes both ways, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: We can provide information to these businesses, but also information to handlers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I am blind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: So that information needs to be accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: So that could mean it's screen reader accessible in a digital format that is accessible to me or even, you know, ASL, whatever people need to be able to do to actually review this information is important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: And specifically for this bill, this material is reviewed every three years and service animal handlers need to have a seat at that table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Like this is not something we can be consulted about afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: This is something we need to be in the room for so that we can make the appropriate changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: So thank you so much for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I have a

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what is said when Mehta is denied entry with her guide dog. Mehta says no documentation is required, describes a restaurant hostess asking her to leave because other customers might be uncomfortable, and says denials also happen at grocery stores, malls, movie theaters, and public agencies.
chapters.title: Hanif asks Masa Mehta about denial conversations and establishments

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: question for Mossom.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So thank you for sharing your testimony with us today and particularly about some of the experiences getting denied entry with your service dog.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share what

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What are, what's being said during those conversations?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And when you're showing maybe your, that this dog who's accompanied you is a service animal, what's the exchange?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: There's a couple different scenarios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Just to clarify, there is no documentation for service animals and a business cannot ask you legally for that documentation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I personally have an ID card that was issued from my guide dog school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: But again, that is a courtesy that is not required.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I usually show that just so they stop yelling at me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: But again, that is not something that is required.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Generally, I will, I'll get kind of a broad gambit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: The last time in recent memory, I was denied.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I went into a restaurant and I approached the counter to be seated and the hostess told me that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: that I just needed to leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: And I was a little confused as to what factor I was being asked to leave about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: But he specifically mentioned that he felt that the other customers at the restaurant would be uncomfortable with my service animal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: So unfortunately, they would not be able to serve me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I was not able to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: educate at the time in a way that he was able to, I guess, take in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I did ask for his manager.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I'm suspicious that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Actually communicate to the manager because he did come back and tell me the chef himself said that I also needed to leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: So it was a bit awkward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I think that generally also one thing that we have to think about here is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: It might not be a conversation of, oh, you have an emotional support animal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: A lot of times the conversation is just no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: And that's it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So what I'm hearing is a combination of restaurant management protocol with or without.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Justified reason, just kind of like just saying no, but then also this element of the other patrons in our establishment are uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So this combination of businesses not knowing that you don't have to provide documentation and that you are

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: allowed to be in their establishment with your service dog and also others who are in the restaurant not knowing that you are indeed allowed to be in that restaurant with your service animal.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So this like necessity of their needing to be broad public education

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: detailing what the rules are around this is absolutely clear from what you have just shared.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so have there been establishments outside of restaurants that...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You or others in your community have experienced denials?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Retail establishments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I have been denied from several small local grocery stores.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I know that members of my community have been denied from shopping malls, movie theaters, public agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: You name it across the board.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether the panel wants to amend Intro 1107. Mehta says the language is good and should stay broad, and Hanif asks the name of Mehta's service dog, who is Mandy.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about bill amendments and service dog name

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And is there, and this can be for anyone on the panel since you all mentioned this bill in your testimony, anything in the bill language that you would want to amend or include in terms of establishments?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Go for it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Anybody who, awesome.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I didn't know if anyone else wanted the mic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I think that the language is good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: I think generally where people have access to public establishments is kind of where this is going to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Really matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: So I think keeping that language broad is important too.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And before I let this panel go, what is your service dog's name?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Her name is Mandy.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mandy, for joining us and for being such a huge supporter of this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Masa Mehta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: We'll move on to the next panel.

chapters.summary: Gary Oye-Steven, a CUNY student and autistic self-advocate, testifies in support of Resolution 510. He describes being socially and systemically excluded as an autistic and intellectually disabled person and as an Indonesian immigrant and queer trans individual.
chapters.title: Gary Oye-Steven supports Autistic Pride Day and shares personal experiences

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hanif and Chair Nurse, for inviting me to testify regarding the Autistic Pride Day Resolution, Resolution 510-2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: I am Gary Oye-Steven.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: I'm a CUNY student, and I used to be a student, but now a graduate from NYCPS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: Today, it is an honor for me to reiterate the importance of socially and systemically affirming the autistic population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: As an autistic and intellectually disabled individual,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: I experienced being socially and systemically passed on, excluded, and overlooked by both neurotypical individuals and even autistic individuals with lower support needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: I have to deal with having to read the room or feel like I don't belong and just

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: question, do I even belong in the space when I have to constantly deal with my peers or staff who lean towards those peers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: or anyone else as a CUNY student or even in my past NYCPS institutions passing me over to others just because I don't socially conform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: Another thing, as an Indonesian individual and a person of immigrant descent,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: I face cultural barriers when trying to find an autistic community that would be able to support me due to experiencing certain neuroaffirming groups that dominate towards Western norms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: Experiences and voices over those who might come from different backgrounds, especially those from collectivist backgrounds like myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: Also, as a queer and trans individual, I even struggle in trying to find a community that would accept me for my sexual orientation or gender identity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: when others in the LGBTQ plus community see me as incapable or

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: not qualified enough of expressing my own identity in the way they see it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: This is why we definitely must use Autistic Pride Day to encourage ongoing and meaningful education,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: academia, training, reform, and widespread encouragement until every autistic individual

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: or every neurotype of all diverse support needs levels is universally affirmed in our society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: We must also encourage continuous progress, education, academia, training, reform, and widespread encouragement in cultural, social,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: and all other labels and competencies until every autistic individual or every person of all cultural and social identities is universally affirmed in society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: My biggest ambition and goal is to build a human rights career in the United Nations in order to connect my experiences,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: knowledge, and advocacy to their mission on reducing inequality and advancing inclusion for disabled individuals all over the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: I am trying to enter youth opportunities and majors in global affairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: I'm currently

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: and applying for certain youth opportunities there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Oye-Steven
utterances.text: Again, thank you, Chair Hanif and Chair Nurse, for letting me testify today.

chapters.summary: Madeline Reichman, staff attorney at the Legal Aid Society and former CCHR attorney, says CCHR needs more funding to enforce disability protections in housing and shelter. She describes class actions against CAMBA and DHS and says disability discrimination is endemic in the shelter system.
chapters.title: Madeline Reichman testifies on Legal Aid, CCHR funding, and shelter discrimination

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: My name is Madeline Reichman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: I'm a staff attorney in the Civil Law Reform Unit at the Legal Aid Society and a former agency attorney at the Commission on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Thank you to Chairs Hanif and Nurse for hosting this oversight hearing on CCHR's disability enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: As we all know, New York City has the broadest anti-discrimination law in the nation and very strong protections for people with disabilities, but the law is only as good as its enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: We strongly believe that CCHR needs additional funding to adequately enforce the city human rights law's disability protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: everywhere, but particularly in housing and shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: The Legal Aid Society takes as many disability rights cases as we can, but we're unable to take on every type of case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: In particular, we've settled class actions against CAMBA, Inc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: For

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: failing to offer reasonable accommodations to their supportive housing tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: We're currently litigating a group case against one of the city's worst landlords in Brooklyn for severe outages of a wheelchair lift and elevators in the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And we're currently monitoring the settlement agreement in our Butler litigation, which is a class action brought against the New York City Department of Homeless Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: for disability discrimination against disabled New Yorkers experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And I would like to flag later on in my testimony the need for increased enforcement in the homeless shelter system where disability discrimination is endemic despite our litigation.

chapters.summary: Reichman says the city human rights law uniquely requires landlords to pay for physical modifications, unlike federal and state law. She says CCHR has only 13 attorneys and nine pre-complaint intervention staff, which is not enough to secure quick relief.
chapters.title: Madeline Reichman explains CCHR unique housing role and staffing shortage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: The Commission on Human Rights has such an important role to play, particularly in housing, because under federal and state law,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: housing providers can't be held liable for failing to make physical modifications to the building unless the tenant is willing to fund those modifications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And only if they're feasible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So the city human rights law is unique in imposing these obligations on landlords and requiring landlords to pay for modifications to buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And the need for modifications to older rent-stabilized buildings in the city is only going to increase as our population ages in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: These tenants come to Legal Aid Society for help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Again, we cannot take all of these cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And many of these tenants rely on Social Security disability income and cannot afford to pay private attorneys to litigate these cases, making the commission one of their only options.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: I do want to flag that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: that in homeless shelters, we would like to see more commission enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: The majority of people in shelter have disability access needs that are not getting met despite systemic reforms in the system brought about by our class action litigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And then just to touch on staffing at the commission,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: It's the sole government agency enforcing the city human rights law, and it's a right-to-file agency, but it simply does not have enough staff to effectively fulfill this mandate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: We heard earlier that currently there are 13 agency attorneys, I believe, and altogether nine staffers in the pre-complaint intervention unit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Which is simply not enough staff to secure quick relief for all of the complainants who come to the commission for help for immediate necessary accommodations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Investing in the commission's enforcement capacity ensures that the protections guaranteed under the law are real for New Yorkers with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Evan Yankey, advocacy director at Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled, says CCHR complaints often lead to years of inaction. He supports Intro 1107 but urges increased funding for MOPD, and supports Intro 131 and the UNCRPD and Autistic Pride resolutions.
chapters.title: Evan Yankey supports Intro 1107, MOPD funding, and Intro 131

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I'm Evan Yinky, and I'm Advocacy Director of the Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled, an independent living center supporting people with disabilities in Brooklyn and beyond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: And I, for visual description, I'm a white man in my 40s wearing a blue suit jacket, a gray plaid shirt, glasses, and medium length brown hair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: We wanted to thank the City Council Disability Committee and its staff for holding this hearing and for being a forum for disability issues in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: And a personal thanks to Chair Hanif, who has been a principled supporter of our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: We support the Council's focus on the City's Commission on Human Rights at today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: The Commission must strengthen its commitment to protecting the rights of disabled New Yorkers by increasing the number of staff devoted to protecting our rights,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: more aggressively following up on complaints, and pursuing legal and legislative action in response to systemic patterns of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: While the rhetoric from the Commission is typically supportive of our rights, complaints to the Commission often lead to years of inaction or proposed settlements that do not result in real change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: It's time for a new approach at the Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: We support Intro 1107, which would require the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, in consultation with the Commission on Civil Rights and the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, to develop guidance and public education campaign on service animal access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: However, we must urge that this important work

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: come with increased funding for MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: We agree that MOPD can and should play a major role in creating city policy, but it must have adequate resources to do the job well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: MOPD is severely underfunded, as documented in a 2022 report by the Center for an Urban Future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: The report showed that New York City spent significantly less per capita on funding for city disability office than other major cities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: This targeted austerity shows up in the ongoing barriers people with disabilities face in accessing city services in a barrier-free life in communities of their choice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: Intro 1107 is welcome legislation in support of the many service animal users who face barriers to access in their daily life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: We think the city should be making an effort on public education, but we also think that city agencies must actively do more to enforce access when people are denied entry to spaces or services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: This is especially true for for-hire vehicles, including Uber and Lyft and local car services, which routinely and illegally deny use by service animal users.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: The city also can play a role in ensuring that people with disabilities who have service animals have a way of seeking recourse when dealing with landlords and housing managers who discriminate against them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: In developing its guidance, we urge the city to consult closely with our community and specifically with the representatives of the blind community and mental health community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: We also urge the city to pass Intro 0131, particularly in the wake of increased...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: increased threats and challenges from the federal government against transgender, gender nonconforming, and intersex New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: Washington and some states have used their targeting of transgender people to undermine established disability protections, including enforcement of federal Section 504 rules, and it is important the city makes every effort to protect access for all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: We are thankful for the resolutions in support of Autistic Pride Day and ratifications of the Convention on the Rights of People with Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: These are both areas where the city can do more in publicizing the barriers that people face and establishing affirmative rights for autistic New Yorkers and other people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: And just on a personal note, I'm an autistic adult and a member of Autistic Adults NYC, which is, as far as we can tell, the largest autistic-led group that has ever existed in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: You know, we hope this committee and the city can work more with that group and give them more increased funding for all the work they do to break down barriers for autistic adults in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: And once again, we urge you to move forward with plans to more fairly fund MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankey
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sherry Yvette Barnett says her daughter died four months ago and she is caring for her son with disabilities. She describes being yelled at, bullied, and treated inhumanely while trying to get food stamps and other services, and asks who will help her.
chapters.title: Sherry Yvette Barnett testifies on daughter's death and mistreatment seeking services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: My name is Sherry Yvette Barnett.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm a little nervous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Understand, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Four months ago, my daughter.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Do you want to take a minute?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then speak into the mic so that we can all hear you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Do you need any water?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: My daughter passed away four months ago of a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: So I'm here today because I was supposed to have been with her, but unfortunately I'm here because my daughter had a disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I have one and my son.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: So it's just my son now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Altogether, I had four children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I only have three boys who are grown.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: My 25-year-old, Reef, I help with him and, you know, take care of him and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: So I'm here because...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: When I try to get services for him or I, you know, turn away or treat it inhumane, told, yelled at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: For instance, I'm trying to get food stamps or anything for him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Let's be real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: They treat me really bad, yell at me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Tell me no, even cut them off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: So I don't know how to get any for next month or the months after.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: During this time, I'm also treated, bully, harass, spit on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: And these are people that are professional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: That's doing this to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I got a call the other day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: They're asking me about...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: What's your name?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: You know, things of that sort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: But what I'm trying to say is when can someone really, who's listening?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I have a disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: These people have power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Who do you think they're going to listen to, me or them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: So I want to know, where can I get some help?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: And also, can someone understand?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: These people, they come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I don't want to say their names in general.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: They come and they just take everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I don't have the important documents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Who stole them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Who did this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: But unfortunately, I'm just being treated really bad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I get no help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm talked down to, like I said, spit on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm a human being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: You're talking about AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Once you say AI, I'm leaving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Because I'm not a fan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm not a fan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I just want my things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: And I'm a citizen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: So why are you questioning me where I'm from, this and that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: You understand?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: So I just want people to understand how many times you're going to bully me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: What about my son?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm coming in the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I can't get upstairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm aching.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm hurting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Just because I look a certain way, trust me, I'm feeling the pain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Plenty of times, my daughter, she's in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: We had to stay downstairs because she couldn't get upstairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: She don't want to hurt herself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: But who's going to help me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Who am I going to tell this to?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: When is it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: gonna stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Just give me, just give me my things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: She's no longer

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I have a son.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: He needs me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: But who's really listening?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm tired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm hurt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I just want my documents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I've been here 40 something years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I got enough sense to know to become a citizen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Why you keep coming for me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Women, you come, you're groping me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: For what?

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks Barnett for her courage and extends condolences on her daughter's death. She says committee staff will connect with Barnett to identify her council member and address delays.
chapters.title: Hanif responds to Sherry Barnett with condolences and staff follow-up

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Sherry, for joining us at today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Signing up to speak and sharing very courageously just the pains that you're experiencing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You should not have to experience any of that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to also just extend our deepest condolences on your daughter's tragic, untimely passing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I know that we have your...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Information and we'll immediately make sure that someone on our staff connects with you so that we know who your council member is to get you

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: to just check into what is what what are the reasons for the various delays and get you back on track but we thank you for joining us

chapters.summary: Barnett says she is in pain and government officials are mistreating her. She describes asking for food stamps, having documents taken, waiting outside for housing help, and being treated like garbage despite having Section 8.
chapters.title: Sherry Barnett continues on housing, documents, and mistreatment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Please, like I said, I'm hurting because I'm tired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: My body aches every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: These are government officials that's doing this to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I asked the lady, I said, do you want me to beg for the stamps because I have to feed my son?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I said, my son doesn't go outside because where we are,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: It's hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: It's like New Jack City.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: But he's not used to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm not used to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I asked for if I can get housing connect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I have Section 8.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: They laugh at me when I go there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I have to stay outside two hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'm a human being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Why would I lie to anyone?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I mean, you treat me like garbage.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, no, and you should absolutely not be treated like garbage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: You knock me down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Sometimes I can't even feel my feet, so I have to put them on the cold floor just to get a little friction in them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: And I'm tired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I just want my documents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We're going to get you back on track.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And Emmett or Fran from our teams are here.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We'll connect with you right away.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks Gary Oye-Steven for his advocacy and asks Madeline Reichman to elaborate on disability discrimination in DHS shelters. Reichman says most shelter residents have disability-related needs and accommodation requests range from air conditioning to single rooms and kitchens.
chapters.title: Hanif thanks Gary and asks Madeline about DHS shelter discrimination

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Before I ask some follow-up questions, my colleagues, any questions?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: First, I just want to thank Gary for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Councilmember One gave you a huge shout-out in her remarks.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: She's not here with us, but she acknowledged just your advocacy in getting us this resolution.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And we look forward to getting the bill passed as soon as possible, but really welcome

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: your advocacy and your activism and also just the CUNY pride as a former CUNY student myself.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Really appreciate you joining us for all the work that you've been doing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I have a question for Madeline.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Madeline.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Madeline.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: On the DHS shelters and the discrimination when it comes to people with disabilities,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you just go a little bit more into that issue?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Yes, Chair Honey, if I'd be happy to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So according to the city's statistics and many different sets of statistics, the majority of shelter residents who are experiencing homelessness

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: have some type of disability-related need that requires some type of accommodation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Many accommodation requests that we see include air conditioning, wheelchair accessible facilities, kitchens, single rooms, emotional support animals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: It really runs the gamut.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Because of our class action, the Department of Homeless Services has developed a process for reasonable accommodation decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: However, we're now about nine years into the settlement agreement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: We're currently negotiating an extension of the agreement so that the city and DHS can come into compliance, but we're still seeing countless denials of reasonable accommodations every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Our homeless rights project receives

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: you know, up to, you know, five or more complaints per day on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And we're simply not able to take on every single caller who comes to us with a reasonable accommodation need in the shelter system.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether rejections are detailed and whether there is an appeal. Reichman says determination notices are vague, appeals sometimes succeed, and even approved accommodations like single rooms or kitchen access often cannot be fulfilled due to limited supply.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about DHS denials, appeals, and unfulfilled accommodations

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The rejections are being detailed in a letter.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And is there an appeal?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So there is an appeals process that we help complainants with as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Usually determination notices don't provide a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So most often they just say that there has not been sufficient medical documentation to establish a need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: The attorneys in our project need to follow up for more details or an actual explanation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
