utterances.text: We do sometimes see different decisions on appeal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Another major problem, though, is that even when DHS approves some accommodations, they simply cannot fulfill them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So, for example, there just aren't many single rooms available in the shelter system, yet we see a huge need for these rooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: From people who are immune compromised, people who have mental health disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: There are really a wide variety of conditions that might require a single room or a kitchen access, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And DHS simply does not have capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: In their system, they simply don't have those available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So what we see is some people have approved accommodations that remain unfulfilled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: We also see a lot of issues with training at the shelter level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So even though there are policies that promote disability access,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: you know, people's lived experiences are quite different and they,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: received discriminatory comments from staff members at these sites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And, you know, we try to flag those for follow-up training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: But, you know, there are hundreds of sites in the DHS portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And, you know, these are really systemic issues that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: We need more enforcement on.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what areas of accommodation are denied and whether people leave shelters when denied. Reichman says single rooms for women in Manhattan and kitchen access are major shortages, and some people leave the shelter system rather than remain in inaccessible facilities.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about denied accommodation areas and shelter exits

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And what are some of the areas in which accommodations are being denied?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So you mentioned anyone who might be immunocompromised, like a single room, requesting a room for themselves, that could be something that

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: gets denied.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are there other sort of like broad topic areas that could be systemic, could be pushed for systemic changes outside of the settlement that they're supposed to adhere to?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Yes, and just to clarify, DHS does have a policy of approving single rooms for people who are immune compromised, but there is a limited supply and people have to wait a long time for them and people who have other types of disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What's the length of time?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So, for example, there are no single rooms available for women in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And so some people will have a location-based reasonable accommodation if they need to be close to medical providers in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So if you...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: identify as a woman and you have both of these RAs, there simply just isn't anything available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And you will just have to wait really until there is, you know, potentially more construction or whatever DHS has to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: One big issue that we're seeing lots of denials for is with kitchens, getting access to a refrigerator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: There's a very limited supply of kitchens in the shelter system that mostly goes to families with children, but only a small percentage of those families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: So really anyone who has some type of disability-related need,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: regarding food and food preparation, people with Crohn's disease or other types of medical conditions,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: they simply are not getting access to kitchens and often may not get approved to bring in their own food into the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Now, when...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Folks are getting denied accommodations, do they tend to remain in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Or is there...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are we also dealing with folks who are leaving the shelter system and then becoming completely unhoused?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Yes, so I don't have statistics, but we do believe that there are some people who are choosing to leave the shelter system when they can't get accommodated rather than remain in inaccessible facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: And we believe that this has been happening with the recent move of the intake site for single adult men from

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: Bellevue to 83rd Street, which is an inaccessible building that the city is currently trying to remediate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Reichman
utterances.text: We do believe that there are likely people who are coming to intake who are then leaving because they are not getting adequately screened or getting the accommodations that they need.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks the panel and calls the third panel: Erika Lorshbough, Alicia Roth-Weigel, Alistair Iddleson, Liat Feller, and Jennifer Levine.
chapters.title: Hanif calls third public testimony panel

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to this panel.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I would like to call our third panel, Erica Lorschbo, Alicia Roth-Weigel, Alistair Iddleson, Liat Feller, Jennifer Levine.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You all can begin when you're ready, in whichever order.

chapters.summary: Erika Lorshbough, executive director of Interact, says intersex people face high rates of discrimination. She says Intro 131 would make anti-discrimination protections explicit in the city human rights law and build on CCHR's historic administrative recognition.
chapters.title: Erika Lorshbough testifies for Intro 131 and intersex protections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I'll go ahead and start because I'm on the end.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Hi, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: My name is Erica Lorschbaugh.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Any pronouns are fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Most folks use they or she.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And I'm a proud queer, intersex, and genderqueer New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I'm also the executive director of Interact, the nation's largest intersex advocacy organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: On behalf of Interact, we so appreciate the chairs bringing Intro 131 onto today's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Intersex variations can look many different ways, but as a group, intersex people face some of the highest rates of discrimination in the community,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: often higher than other groups in the LGBTQ plus umbrella, and more than triple the rate of all people of any sexual orientation or gender identity who don't have intersex traits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Councilmember Caban's bill, Intro 131, would make anti-discrimination protections for intersex people explicit on the face of the city human rights law, including in housing, employment, and public accommodations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Years ago, the City Commission on Human Rights broke ground for the intersex folks who live in, work in, and visit our city by extending the law's sex and gender-based protections to people with intersex traits through administrative decision-making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: This was a genuinely historic move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: We celebrated it, and it cut a path that many other jurisdictions have followed since, including New York State.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: But back then, nobody could anticipate the vicious attacks that our community faces today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: These attacks on basic human sex and gender diversity are primarily aimed at trans people, especially trans women, but they have an equally intense and often invisible or poorly understood impact on intersex people as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Making anti-discrimination protections plain and permanent in the city code will help intersex New Yorkers understand and embrace their rights, and it will inform employers, businesses, and housing providers as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: It's a simple move in a way, thanks to the Commission's existing interpretation, but for a community that disproportionately experiences invisibility, exclusion, and discrimination, this clarity and permanence in the law can make a genuine difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And a genuine difference is what is needed now for intersex people more than ever before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: size of our democracy, we don't rest on administrative action when fundamental rights are under assault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: We gather the political will to enshrine our values of equality as permanent law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: We have the will, and the need is evident, and now is the time for this council to make New York City a leader on intersex rights once again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Interact thanks the Civil and Human Rights Committee for hearing Intro 131 today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: We thank the Commission for their support, and we urge the Council to pass this law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: We're so grateful to you all for your time and support.

chapters.summary: Alicia Roth Weigel, CUNY adjunct faculty and intersex person, says New York City has been vital in intersex history. She describes healthcare inequity, forced surgeries, and the need for explicit statutory protection and intersex-specific care.
chapters.title: Alicia Roth Weigel testifies on intersex history and healthcare inequity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Howdy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: My name is Alicia Roth-Weigel, and I don't usually read.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I usually just speak off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I didn't know I had four minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: This feels like a luxury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I have twice the time, so I'm going to take like a breath.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So yeah, my name is Alicia Roth-Weigel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I'm testifying today as adjunct faculty at CUNY, where I teach a course on sex and gender in Hunter College's sociology department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So would consider myself an expert professionally in this regard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Also personally as an intersex person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And I'm also speaking as a former resident of Williamsburg, Brooklyn, which I can tell you looks quite different than when I lived there over a decade ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Certainly wasn't an Apple store.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: But one face that does look familiar to me is Councilmember Caban.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Who has been working on the issue of intersex autonomy for five plus years now, at least since she attended a rally that I co-organized at Weill Cornell Medical College back in 2021 and was attended and worked on by multiple other people

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: in this room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: We have been fighting this fight for a very long time and appreciate Councilmember Caban's ongoing support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: That protest was also featured in...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: the Emmy-nominated documentary Everybody, which premiered at Tribeca Film Festival.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So all of this is to say that New York City has been and continues to be vital in the course of intersex history, which thus far has been ignored by most of the world, but one day will make it into history books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I was originally connected with Councilmember Caban while serving on the City of Austin's Human Rights Commission, where I served for eight years before moving here to, as I mentioned, now teach at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And at that time, serving on Austin's Human Rights Commission, we worked to incorporate language from New York City's 2019 legal enforcement guidance on discrimination into all of Austin's local non-discrimination ordinance policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So we did codify intersex protection into city law, but with reference to hormonal and chromosomal differences without explicitly referencing our community by name.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And while this change might seem minor, might seem incremental, it's not for a largely invisible community

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: who has pretty much always been ignored and whose needs sometimes overlap with that of transgender individuals, though not always.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And yet we are frequently, and this is me going off the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: cuff again, lumped in with protections for trans folks in ways that don't adequately meet our medical needs, our

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: unique needs in terms of protection from discrimination that, again, often overlap with transgender folks, but often do not and are unique to intersex people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So our struggle has always been lumped into that one rather than being seen as valid and acted on in its own right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And so I think explicitly listing us as a protected class would be an important step in the right direction, that we are also a valid community that deserves human rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: In that vein, beyond legal statute, this body could make a tangible difference in many lives by helping to bring Callan Lord to the table to rectify the huge health care inequity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: faced by intersex people through the provision of intersex-specific care for adult patients, which would be replicating work that we pioneered via kind clinics across the state of Texas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Again, this work has already been done in Texas, mind you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And so I feel like we could easily do it in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: We just need Callan Lord to reply to intersex people slash care about intersex people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I'd be happy to provide guidance on that or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And I thank you for reaffirming that in the absence of federal representation, we can still make big things happen through the power of local organizing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So thanks for listening.

chapters.summary: Liat Fowler, president of Interconnect Support Group, says she was fired without explanation after her intersex trait became visible. She says explicit protection is needed so intersex people know their legal recourse and are not left undefined in anti-discrimination law.
chapters.title: Liat Fowler testifies on being fired for intersex traits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: If it's red, does that mean it's on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Yeah, cool.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Thank you all for the opportunity to speak and share my story today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: My name is Liat Feller, and I find many of my communities here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: A visual description of myself for those who might need that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I'm a white presenting Jewish intersex woman in my mid-20s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I have long brown hair that hangs past my broad shoulders and desperately needs a haircut.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And bright colored glasses on my face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Typically, I sport a full beard, but it just so happens this week I am clean shaven.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I'm a part-time wheelchair user, and I'm wearing a bright purple blazer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Which people say is the color of my aura.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And I use she, her, or they, them pronouns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I'm also president of Interconnect Support Group, the national peer support network for intersex folks and their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And today I'm testifying on my own behalf as an intersex woman in strong support of Introduction 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: With federal protections for intersex people having been completely rolled back by the current administration, comprehensive state and local protections are more crucial now than ever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: To write explicit intersex protection into law would be to affirm our basic existence, something that should never have to be debated, but still so often is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Much of the harm and isolation that intersex people experience stems from ignorance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Ignorance, misunderstanding, or disbelief that we exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: To be intersex is a natural phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: We're not some myth, and we're not freaking unicorns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Though I know an intersex five-year-old who would like to be one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: When I came out to my mother, she cried.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Not out of disappointment, but out of fear for how the world would treat me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: She knew that without explicit legal protection for intersex folks, people would continue to pathologize our bodies, misunderstand our experiences of gender and sex, and deny our sheer existence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: My mom is wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: When COVID mask mandates were lifted in 2021, I was a young teacher in the observant faith community that I was raised in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Going to work without a mask for the first time, since coming out as intersex, meant that my most prominent intersex trait, a full beard rivaling that of my brother, the Hasidic rabbi, was on full display for the first time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: That week, I was fired without explanation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Because intersex traits were not explicitly defined in anti-discrimination law, I didn't know my clear legal recourse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I wasn't fired for being a woman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I was fired for being intersex, and visibly so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Friends stopped looking me in the eye.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: My community isolated me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I lost more than eight weeks'worth of income, and I've since left classroom teaching entirely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Ignorance breeds discrimination, and discrimination thrives when it's left undefined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I'm asking you to explicitly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: affirm intersex existence, and define our rights so that equal protection under the law becomes non-negotiable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: New York City was a national leader when the CCHR recognized intersex traits as protected via interpretation of existing anti-discrimination laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: The city has an opportunity to be a national leader again by modeling what it looks like to value and protect intersex people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Wholly, firmly, and proudly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Please pass Introduction 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Jennifer Levine, board member of Interconnect, says she was told to keep her intersex variation secret and had no resources or support. She describes finding community through Interconnect and asks the Council to pass Intro 131.
chapters.title: Jennifer Levine testifies on shame, secrecy, and Interconnect support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: My name is Jennifer Levine and I use she, her, or they, them pronouns for a visual description.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I am a tall, frizzy-haired redhead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I'm quite loud most of the time, but I'll try to keep it to a minimum today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I'm an intersectional New Yorker and sitting board member of Interconnect, the nation's largest support network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Today, I am speaking on my own behalf in support of Intro 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Like many marginalized groups, intersex people are not a monolith.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Each person has a unique story, unique life experience, and deals with their own set of difficulties, be they health-related, career-related, or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Among the many stories I have heard in the six years I have worked with Interconnect, one theme has been consistent, shame, secrecy, and isolation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: As a young person, after learning about my intersex variation, I was told by doctors, family members, and trusted leaders in my community to keep it a secret, to not tell any friends or extended family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: To an extroverted teenager like me, this was tantamount to a punishment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I was forbidden to discuss this thing I had learned about my body with my closest friends and allies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: The word cancer was mentioned and a surgery was suggested, but my mother gave me the option to wait, and I did, and I'm glad I did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: No additional resources were given.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: No support was provided.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And no introductions to other young people like me were made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Sorry, I lost my mother a few months ago.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: There's a tissue box.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Speaking about her is very hard for me.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: No, take your time, too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: For years, I held on to this secret, describing it as my infertility issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I'm using air quotes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Or my problem when discussing things with my mom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: She would always say, but you haven't told anybody, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And I would always let her know yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Even as I entered college and then entered the workforce, I had this...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I held this so quietly, even after revealing to trusted friends or partners that I may die from cancer at some point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I never shared the full truth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Lack of representation also led me to believe that my issue, again I'm using air quotes, must be rare and that people couldn't understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: It wasn't until years later.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Excuse me, I lost my place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: It wasn't until years later when I realized how angry and frustrated I was all the time that I started to dig deeper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I was so heavily medicalized that I thought only doctors could give me the answers I sought after.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: But when I found this support group that would become Interconnect, I realized there were other people like me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I wasn't alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I met with a group of women, several of whom are still good friends today, and realized our stories may be different, but they were also so similar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Once I attended my first national gathering for the group, I knew I wanted to help organize, provide resources, help with the outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I could make a difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: To make sure people felt less alone, stigmatized, or shameful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: The work of Interconnect, an organization that has existed in one form or another for 30 years, is vital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: We provide support services, networking, programming, and online education to families, young people, parents, allies, and healthcare providers so they understand how intersex people deserve to live authentically and with purpose, not shamefully or alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Our motto is be seen with seen acronymically representing supported, embraced, educated, and networked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I think the most important part of that is embraced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Because if I had just one person, just one single friend or community member to say, hey, there's nothing wrong with you, you don't need to be fixed, and your body is beautiful, I may not have hid like that for as long as I did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: My work within the community has shown me that so many of us were told the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: You know, the other kids aren't going to understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Or maybe don't tell your partner about that until you have to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Forcing an already marginalized person to hide a part of themselves, I think that's shameful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: This city is built on diversity and inclusion, a shining beacon of a skyline that has welcomed people for centuries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Our laws should be just as welcoming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: For that reason, I ask the council to pass Intro 131, and thank you for your time and consideration.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Right on the dot.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm a pro.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all so much for showing up today and for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I've just learned so much, not only from the bill that Councilmember Caban has put forward, and I'm so grateful that it's getting heard today.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We're going to get it passed.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But just learned so much from all of your testimonies.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Proud CUNY graduate from Brooklyn College.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I was a women's and gender studies major and an LGBTQ studies minor.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So grateful that CUNY has the discipline on these issues and that we've got great educators who are leading the charge on these issues.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to pass it to Councilmember McBond for her questions.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I have, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Oh, I just apologize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: We have one other person who was called up for this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So sorry.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Alistair Henry-Idelson, a civil rights lawyer and trans person with a disability, supports Intro 131. He says intersex status and gender identity are different and explicit standalone protections help intersex people and those perceived as intersex.
chapters.title: Alistair Henry-Idelson testifies for standalone intersex protections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Thanks, all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: The goal is to get...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Apologize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: No, you guys are fab, and these are all rock stars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: So just thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Hey, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to submit testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: It's an honor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: My name is Alistair Henry Idelson, and I live in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And I'm a trans person with an invisible, life-threatening physical disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: I want to thank all of my co-panelists and each of you for the effort, and everyone in this room, because I know it takes a lot to get us here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: I'm speaking, of course, in support of Intro 131, and I've been a civil rights lawyer for more than two decades, most recently with the General Counsel's Office of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Department of Health and Human Services Civil Rights Division, where I was responsible for helping to ensure civil rights compliance in the health programs of the United States.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Under the Biden administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Before that, I was the legal director of Interact, the nation's largest intersex advocacy organization and a main power behind New York City's leading administrative recognition of this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: So I first began working on this issue many years ago in law school, and I was just flabbergasted that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: no one was doing a sufficient job protecting this amazing, beautiful community that was experiencing ongoing horrific harms, what has been called a form of torture by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: As I got to learn more and saw the way intersex people were being treated, I became more convinced that explicit protection was necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And it's part of why Interact engaged with the Human Rights Commission on that crucial guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: So thank you all for everyone here who helped make that happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And part of the reason I'm here today is because that was so many years ago, and we're still seeing the same kind of harms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: We're still saying the same kind of things, so more must be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And particularly, as folks have said, when federal protections to help address this issue have been rolled back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And I know personally how challenging it was to get those passed at the federal level because I was, in fact, trying to get them passed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: So, of course, we can and should be the first legislative body to make standalone protections explicit and permanent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And then just one other thing, intersex status and gender identity are, of course, different aspects of who a person is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And even in my many years of working with experienced and very intelligent attorneys and other folks, many people conflate being intersex with being trans or other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: identities, other ways of being, and clear standalone protections helps not only this group, but also related groups

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: and those who may not be intersex or, you know, other things, but who experience discrimination on the basis of perceived intersex status or perceived intersex traits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: the serious uptick in gender panic, again, as other folks have talked about, this is just more important than ever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: So basically, New York

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: has done an amazing job so far thanks to so many people here, but more is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: So I really appreciate the chance to express support and also for your careful time and consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: And I ask the council to pass intro 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alistair Henry-Idelson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Caban thanks the panel and asks for more examples of discrimination and what CCHR outreach should look like. Panelists describe healthcare discrimination, exclusion within LGBTQIA spaces, gender policing, and the need for public education.
chapters.title: Caban asks panel about discrimination examples and CCHR outreach

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you all so, so much.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's nice to see you all.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Before I ask my questions, I just want to say that I'm thankful and proud that we're here able to hear this legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And Alicia, I was moved by your really kind words because

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I just, I owe a lot to you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I think like my colleagues, we see our work, our public service work is rooted in part of being, you know, liberation work.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And it is our jobs, it is my job to be in community with all people who are in the fight for freedom, for dignity, for health, for safety.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: there's a lot to learn and grow.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And for lots of different issues, I've had sort of like my rabbis, so to speak, you know, for sex work, it was Cecilia Gentile that brought me into that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Who was at that same protest with us, by the way, back in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You know, for Palestinian liberation, it was Sumaya Wad and Linda Sarsour.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And for, you know, the work on behalf of intersex folks, it is you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: These are the people that have taught me not just to be allies in these liberation struggles, but to be co-conspirators.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I owe you a lot.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And my question is for all of you, you can chime in however you'd like, but

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: can you tell us, you've spoken about it some, but if there are more examples that you'd like to give about the kinds of discrimination you have seen or experienced, please feel free to share them.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And in your view, what kind of action should the government take to prevent or address this kind of discrimination?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Specifically, you know, would additional outreach or education on CCR's part, CCHR's part be helpful?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if so, what should that outreach look like?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think Liat's testimony was so powerful in terms of the discrimination based on perceived differences that has been mentioned multiple times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: But the reason I brought Kellen Lord into my conversation is I think health care discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And just healthcare inequity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And even within like LGBTQI plus spaces, they like to tack the eye on, but without necessarily doing anything meaningful to include us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And I don't mean just include us like with like a little rainbow, like whatever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I mean, like get us the healthcare we need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So I've had osteoporosis since my late 20s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: That is like the norm in so much of our community because of inadequate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Hormone care because of surgeries that are forced onto our bodies and fallout from that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: There are so many other physical implications from those surgeries in the short term and long term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And that protest that we led was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: with regard to bad actor doctors who remain active in this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And I would say it is certainly discriminatory to cut children's genitalia without their consent and then use vibrators on them as part of the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: of medical research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: So I think that this would be a big first step to pass this today,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: but I just hope that it is viewed as a first step in a much longer investigatory process and process to pass multiple meaningful forms of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: legislation to protect this community and to adequately meet our health care needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: There's one other thing that I think is interesting in the discrimination conversation, which is, you know, even within the intersex community, there's definitely

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: a logic behind conversations that you have either with employers or doctors or providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: conversation, there's a disparity between quote unquote intact intersex people like myself and people who are then operated on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And I think that's in and of itself, a further level of discrimination that hopefully will be discussed maybe once this is passed or in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: But that gives you a sort of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: insider look into the kinds of imposter syndrome that we have even in our own community, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Where I was afraid to seek out additional support for so long, not just because I was told to keep it a secret and to keep it safe, but also to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: you know, in my own view, you know, seeing different kinds of work,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: that was being done online by Interact, I was like, oh, well, I haven't been surgically altered, so I'm not as, I don't belong with this group of people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: So I think redefining this, the term of gender to include intersex people, but then also talking about intersex people generally as, you know, both

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: medically altered, not medically altered, you know, hormone replaced, not hormone replaced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: There's definitely lots of different levels of treatment and of care that we've received or unfortunately haven't received.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I'd just like to add that, you know, also as a person whose intersex status has not been hyper-medicalized, you know, really

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: my grandmother made an attempt when I was about 9 or 10 and experiencing a precocious puberty that was both virilizing and feminizing and tried to get me on medication and do a bunch of stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And my mom was kind of like, nah, and I was very much like, meh.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So we didn't go that route.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And still at the same time, from about that age, 9 or 10, is how long I have been experiencing just people clocking me as different is how I think about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: You know, my voice was almost as low at that age.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: People thought I was my mother's sister.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And like I if I went into the women's bathroom, I would I would get looks already at that age.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So I think for me, you know, in a way that is actually kind of distinct from the way that the law protects us in our gender identity or expression, you know, like Leah spoke about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: You know, there may be times when I want to sport my mustache and it feels good to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And that's about my gender expression.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And there may be times that it's just on my face and I might get a look if I'm going into the women's restroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And that, you know, it's a fine distinction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And I wouldn't argue that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: that the commission's protections, existing protections, don't cover that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: But, you know, as a civil rights lawyer myself and an intersex person, I kind of have to sit with the fact that they don't cover it because the law contemplated people like us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And I think that, you know, like, again, as a civil rights lawyer, there's just this dignitary thing about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And I know that we're going to do this in New York because, again, like I said, we have the will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I think, you know, I've experienced more gender policing in the city than anywhere I've been.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And it surprises me sometimes because New Yorkers are very, like, live and let live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: You know, I think truly, like for folks who come from out of town or all of us when we're visiting the city's businesses and public accommodations, I honestly think like that protection is going to be really meaningful,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: especially because of the rise of this like moral panic around sex and gender that just doesn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Relate to anything about the actual diversity of human bodies and human presentation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: And as a dog whistle when we all should be focusing on climate change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Oh my gosh.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So yeah, that's my two cents, I think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: What Alicia said about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: healthcare disparities and this phenomenon where we're, you know, even LGBTQIA spaces will say that we're included.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And then it's kind of like, okay, so you said the word intersex, but now what?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I think of an experience I went to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I spend a lot of time here in New York, but I live in Stanford about 45 minutes away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And I went to visit our, and Stanford looks up to New York as, you know, as a role model for a lot of this legislation and stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I went to our LGBTQIA health center that stated intersex care on their website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And I was at a point where I was tired of looking at my medical situation and my hormone profile as something pathological, which is what I was told when I was nine years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: You're doomed to a life of weight loss and chasing a femininity you're never going to have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And you're always going to be hairy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And that's it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And so I went and I shared and I explained that I wanted a more holistic approach and I wanted an approach that was affirming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And I just wanted to be what made my body feel the best, not what shoved it in a box.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And the nurse said to me, so here's the thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: If you were just trans, I could do this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I would know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I could get you from point A to point B.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: But you don't even know where your point A is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And you don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: even know where your point B is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: So I got nothing for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And this was where I was being sent for expertise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And, you know, I'm so thankful for the team that I've built, many of whom are here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: But it was like, it was a huge jolt where I needed to find

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: where I needed to find solace and I needed to find acceptance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: You know, New York City is the first place that a makeup artist at Sephora

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: assumed that my beard was not an accident and assumed that it was who I was meant to be in front of my now 93-year-old grandmother, whom...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: I will never tell her that she's who I learned how to pluck my beard with my fingers from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: But it's also the place where hopping on a train, I'm whispered and cursed at and called a tranny and an effing bearded lady and all of these things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And I think of the impact of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: The explicit recognition of intersex as a protected category.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And it is that example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: It's so that nobody else, you know, works in a faith community and, you know, faith communities, they have their own ways of dealing with, of responding to legislation, but, you know, they can't look at the law of the land and say,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Well, even the regular law doesn't protect you, so why should we?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: And it's about setting that example and setting that expectation that we are worth protection and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liat Fowler
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks which community organizations and health care providers are modeling positive support for intersex New Yorkers. Panelists praise DOHMH, describe finding competent and humble providers, and discuss Interconnect's national gatherings and possible clinical competency work.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about community organizations and health providers modeling support

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I wanted to hear a little bit more about the community organizations and health care providers that are modeling

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: positive support for intersex New Yorkers that this council should know about.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I know Interconnect was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I heard the feedback around Can the Lord needing to be called in.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd love to hear just a little bit more about like who's out there that we should be, we should know about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I will say, honestly, the folks at DOHMH who, you know, tried to get the 2021 education

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: campaign off the ground, it got slashed by Mayor Adams when he was blaming all immigrants for everything and cutting funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I'm blaming the immigrants for that too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So, but they are actually working on it right now, getting it back up and running.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And I legit cannot say enough about the folks at UHMH.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And it's in kind of like the Reproductive Justice and Sexual Health Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I will say I am delighted to hear, Liat, that you are finding competent care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I often am like, I mean, I've seen folks who, again, are supposed to be experts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And, you know, truly, as I enter a new phase of my life,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: the phase, there's nobody who knows what my endocrine profile is supposed to look like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So we're just figuring it out together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And that's actually the thing is that the best care I have received isn't from doctors who thought they knew a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: It's from doctors who knew that they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So they asked deep questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: They actively listened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And they...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: did their own homework in between our visits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Like, truly, I went from an endocrinologist who, you know, mostly worked with people with diabetes, didn't know anything about intersex variations, and she...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Just supported me so well because she knew she wasn't an expert and that she had to rely on some of my own expertise about my experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And I went from there to an absolute expert at a gender clinic at a hospital that I don't want to name, but like this guy,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: was so sure that he knew everything that he actually made a bunch of very serious medical mistakes, including doing things like sending me for a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: dexamethasone suppressed hormone panel, which basically means like the testosterone that my body produces was diminished, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And so then that was supposed to be for comparison.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I came back and I met with him and he said, good news, you're normal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And I was like, oh, there are so many things wrong with what you're saying to me right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And actually, the worst thing isn't that you shouldn't say that to an intersex person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: The worst thing is that you don't remember that this is a dexamethasone suppressed test that you sent me for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And you're just reading it as if these are my everyday.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: endocrine numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: So, um, honestly, I, I, like I, I love specialization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I love expertise, but the people who are humble are, are providing the best care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Um, and yeah, DOHMH, like they are just trying really, really hard to, um,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: absolutely lead in the nation's public health departments on intersex understanding and education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Yeah, on the medical piece, I would say from the years of 2011 to 2021, I was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And so it was such a journey to try to find even one qualified or educated medical professional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: It was a lot of me doing my own advocating and me doing my own educating, which as an intersex person, we can all agree that it is exhausting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: having to over and over explain yourself to someone why you don't have a period, why you don't produce whatever hormone you don't produce, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Someone who went to med school and makes a lot more money than you do who should know those things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Yeah, they should.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: They truly should.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: But it was surprising to me, even as recently as this year, to be connected with an endocrinologist for my diabetes, like a completely unrelated condition, at least not unrelated to my intersex variation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And for me to go in thinking, okay, another time I'm going to have to explain my whole body to this person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And immediately she shut me down and was like, oh, yeah, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And I was like,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: I mean, do you know or do you really know?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And she was like, it's this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: It happens this way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: You experience this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: You experience this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And I was like, blown away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: That's Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Jillian Goddard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Shout out to her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Terrific endocrinologist in the village.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: But beyond the health care side of it, I think the community side of it, Interconnect operates all over the nation, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: We're headquartered in Illinois, technically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: But we do a lot of our work online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: So we're providing a lot of support services on the Internet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And we're providing at least one annual national gathering once per year, usually in July.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: We just had our gathering in July of this year in Connecticut.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: We would love to have it in New York if it wasn't so expensive to have conferences and conventions here, maybe someday.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: We did have our first actual meeting in 1996 in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: And, you know, I think for our future gatherings or in-person support, we'd like to continue to have these regional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: Regional events to support the team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: If there were some way or some co-sponsoring organization or something that y'all are aware of that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Levine
utterances.text: you could connect us with to be able to have those smaller, maybe half-day kind of gatherings, I know that there are a lot of intersex New Yorkers or people in the tri-state area that would be very, very excited about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: One thing I just wanted to add actually was that because health and hospitals was also the first and I guess only public health system in the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: to outright ban non-consensual surgeries on intersex kids and I think also referrals for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I wonder if there isn't something that we could explore in terms of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: clinical intersex competency situated within health and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: You know, that, you know, just sort of like a partnership between DOHMH and the folks who are in the health and hospitals subset.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: I feel like there could be, you know, something to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: And, you know, it wouldn't have to fall on Cal and Lord as a private organization that takes a lot of public funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: It could be a public and publicly funded topic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Yeah, I just know they do take public funding, including city funding.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Our health committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erika Lorshbough
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I was like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: I know we're like short on time and I want to make sure we're germane to this specific ordinance when there's obviously a lot of work that needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: But yeah, happy to speak in other contexts about what was done in Texas and what we might be able to replicate here elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alicia Roth Weigel
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif calls the fourth panel: Elizabeth Cooper, Brian E. Price, Alyssa Ball, Cameron Mukherjee, Hugh Rose Evans, and Alex Valou.
chapters.title: Hanif calls fourth public testimony panel

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Moving on to our fourth panel, I'd like to call Elizabeth Cooper, Brian E.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Price, Alyssa Ball, Cameron, Mokherjee, Hugh, Rose Evans, Alexander, Veyu.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: There should be enough seats to sit by the table.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And anyone can kick us off.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Just speak into the mic.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You'll have to click.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: He turned it off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: Okay, we're good.

chapters.summary: Alyssa Ball, a wellness practitioner and intersex New Yorker, says explicit legal recognition improves mental health and social standing. She describes exclusion and misunderstanding even within LGBTQIA spaces and supports Intro 131.
chapters.title: Alyssa Ball testifies for Intro 131 and intersex visibility

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: My name is Alyssa Ball, and I'm a resident here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: For visual description, I am the tall, hot, intersex person wearing a brown striped shirt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: My pronouns are they, she, and I am a super out and proud intersex person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: I am here speaking in support of Intro 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: I'm a wellness practitioner who serves many people in the LGBTQIA plus community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: So through my work and my own lived experiences, I know firsthand how vital inclusion and well-being are to our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: Having rights acknowledged clearly in the text of law has been shown to improve the mental health and social standing of people in protected groups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: And this is why this legislation is just super important in general for us to be included.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: I dreamed of running away to New York City since I was a little girl.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: I had this big dream of coming to this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: And I think I will always remember my first New York City Pride Parade over 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: And feeling like my days of hiding would finally be over, finding this place of belonging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: So New York to me is that place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: So hopefully that could be reflected here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: New York City is such a special place where it promises us all that we can belong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: But the fight for intersex visibility only continues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: Even within the broader LGBTQIA plus community, we face exclusion and misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: I have been surprised by how many times I've had to explain to people within our own community

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: how intersex is different from transgender and non-binary, or that these are totally different things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: And that intersex really is a beautiful spectrum of characteristics that fall under the intersex umbrella.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: With much frustration, I watched Donald Trump claim in his inauguration speech that there would be two genders recognized by the United States, male and female.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
