utterances.text: And like many people, he doesn't know the difference between biological sex and gender.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: This lack of education creates real-world impact and disadvantages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: Despite his lack of care, intersex people aren't going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: We have always been here and we always will be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: I hope you understand how imperative it is for our experiences to be heard and valued and that we must receive equal consideration under any and all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: So again, I appreciate the chance to express my support and thank the council for supporting Intro 131 and to make anti-discrimination protections for intersex people permanent in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa Ball
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Alex Valou, a Fordham Law student in the legislative advocacy clinic, says Intro 131 would amend Section 8-102 to include intersex traits. He says codifying the existing interpretation prevents future commissions from revoking guidance and protects 140,000 intersex New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Alex Valou testifies on codifying intersex protections in Section 8-102

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: Let me shift this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: My name is Alex Valou, and I am a third-year law student at Fordham University School of Law, and I was participating in our legislative advocacy clinic in the spring 2026 semester, which is part of Lincoln Square Legal Services, Inc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: For the last two years, we have partnered with Interact, an intersex rights advocacy group, which you heard from prior, and its executive director, Arka Lorschbo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: So you have heard from many intersex individuals about their experiences facing discrimination and indignity merely because of who they are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: Today, I will emphasize the need for a statutory amendment to the language of Section 8-102.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: While the interpretive guidelines mention discrimination against intersex people, incorporating intersex traits into the statutory language increases visibility and ensures that advisory guidelines cannot be revoked at a later date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: In 2015, the New York City Commission on Civil and Human Rights promulgated rules to guide enforcement on Section 8-102 of New York City Human Rights Law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: The guidance currently mentions intersex under its definition section and includes the term as an example of violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: In 2019, the Commission...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: The Commission issued additional guidance interpreting the prohibition on gender-based discrimination to include discrimination based on being intersex.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: While the Commission has interpreted discrimination against intersex people to be prohibited, a future Commission or administration may choose to amend the rules or to revoke its guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: So by amending Section 8-102 to include intersex trades, the Council today can prevent any changes in the rule or guidelines tomorrow that may harm the New York City intersex community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: As we all know, the political environment of the United States and the state of New York are in flux.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: New York City has always been a stronghold of human rights with forward-looking laws that ensure protection for the city's diverse inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: Intro 131 is no different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: Intro 131 does not create a new liability regime for the Commission to enforce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: It does not change the Commission's enforcement mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: It codifies an existing interpretation of Section 8-102 to ensure stable protection of a community of 140,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: So to codify and strain the protections for this far too often overlooked segment of New Yorkers, we urge the committee to report this bill to the full council for consideration and for its passage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Valou
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Bryony Price, an intersex educator and Columbia graduate, says she was subjected to non-consensual genital surgery at age two. She describes workplace discrimination, bathroom access barriers, and healthcare hurdles, and supports Intro 131.
chapters.title: Bryony Price testifies on non-consensual surgery and discrimination

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of Intro 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: My name is Bryony Price, and I am an intersex person with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: I'm testifying today on my own behalf, but I'm also a professional member of the Grammy Recording Academy,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: a New York City public school educator, and a Columbia graduate where my research explores intersectional access across arts and education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: As you might hear from my accent, I grew up in the UK.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Like so many intersex people, my earliest memory was being restrained to a hospital bed for a non-consensual, normalizing, quote, genital surgery that left me with lifelong repercussions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: I was two years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: I was too young to understand what was happening, let alone consent to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Yet decisions were made about my body that would affect me for the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: My experience is a part of a much wider history of intersex people being subjected to medical interventions intended to make our bodies conform to societal expectations of what male and female bodies should look like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Whilst living and working in New York for the past nine years, I've experienced discrimination in the workplace, denial of appropriate bathroom access and barriers to health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: But discrimination against intersex people can be nuanced and insidious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: In many medical settings, I've been forced to take pregnancy tests before accessing treatment, despite explaining repeatedly that I have neither ovaries or a uterus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Even in healthcare settings, I find myself having to justify my own anatomy to access medical care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: This is why explicit recognition of intersex traits matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Discrimination isn't always about gender identity or expression.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Sometimes it's about the very characteristics of our bodies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: I've worked in New York City public schools for nine years now, dedicating my time to creating opportunities for young people through education and the arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: During that time, I've witnessed the violence, bullying and discrimination that LGBTQIA young people continue to face, often simply for being themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: As educators, we work to create environments where every student feels safe, valued and able to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Yet even as I've advocated for my students, I felt the pressure to conceal aspects of my own identity for fear of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: And I know I'm not alone in that experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: I invite you to look around at the incredible intersex people testifying today, both in person and online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: We're authors, artists, advocates, lawyers, athletes, educators, musicians, and so much more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Like everyone else, we want the freedom to participate fully in society, including in sport.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Yet intersex athletes have faced in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: invasive scrutiny, exclusion and demands to medically alter their natural bodies simply to compete.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: We should not have to choose between participating in society and preserving our bodily autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Through my Recording Academy membership, I work to build greater visibility for intersex musicians and artists, but visibility alone is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: We cannot meaningfully participate in society if we must first conceal who we are to feel safe within it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: New York City was a pioneer in recognizing intersex discrimination through administrative guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Intro 131 offers an opportunity to make these protections explicit in human rights law, giving intersex New Yorkers clearer recognition and a stronger foundation for challenging discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: At a time when our bodies and identities are so politicized, we must ensure they cannot be weaponized against.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: This legislation is about more than legal language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: It's about ensuring future generations of intersex New Yorkers can live without shame, fear or discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Hugh Rose Evans speaks for the American LGBTQ Museum in support of Intro 131. He says intersex people are valued parts of the LGBTQIA community and deserve explicit, permanent protection under the law.
chapters.title: Hugh Rose Evans supports Intro 131 for American LGBTQ Museum

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Ooh, great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: My name is Hugh Rose Evans, and I'm speaking on behalf of the American LGBTQ Museum in support of Intro 131 to codify anti-discrimination protections for intersex people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: I speak today as an ally, and I want to thank Interact for the invite to speak along with them today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Our museum proudly acknowledges that intersex people are a valued part of the LGBTQI plus community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: They make history every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Just take the testimonies from my colleagues that have spoken here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: They're artists, they're cultural musicians, they're directors, they're people who contribute to our everyday society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Yet we live in a world that seeks to erase their very existence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Our intersex colleagues, friends, and family members deserve equal recognition and equal protection under the law because they indeed are our colleagues, friends, and family members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: They exist, and they're not alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Having rights acknowledged clearly in the text of the law has been shown to improve the mental health and social standing of people in protected groups and classes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: And because intersex people struggle against invisibility and high rates of discrimination, these benefits are even more impactful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: This is an incredible opportunity for our city to stand up for what's right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Historically, New York was the first city in the United States to extend broad protections against sex and gender-based discrimination to intersex people under the city's Human Rights Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: And now the NYC Council has the opportunity to be the first legislative body to make standalone protections for intersex people explicit and permanent in its human rights statute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: We at the museum want to thank everyone on the committee today, the people who've testified in support, and of course, Councilmember Caban for supporting and sponsoring Intro 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: And we wholeheartedly believe in the council's ability to pass this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time and consideration of all our testimonies.

chapters.summary: Cameron Mukherjee, a Fordham Law student, says 140,000 intersex New Yorkers face under-enforcement because the protection is only in guidance. He says Intro 131 is a simple amendment that clarifies the law without creating new liability.
chapters.title: Cameron Mukherjee testifies on under-enforcement and explicit statutory reference

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Thank you to the chairs, Councilmember Nurse and Councilmember Hanif, for giving us the opportunity to speak about this key legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: And of course, thank you to Councilmember Kaban for introducing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: My name is Cameron Mukherjee, and I'm a third-year student in Fordham Law School and participate in our legislative advocacy clinic, which is part of Lincoln Square Legal Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: For the last two years, we have partnered with Interact, an intersex advocacy group, and its executive director, Erica Lorschba.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: You have heard from many intersex individuals about their experiences facing discrimination and indignity merely because of who they are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Approximately 140,000 New Yorkers are intersex, and they deal with similar struggles every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: By explicitly protecting intersex people from discrimination, the Council will be making a lasting statement that New York City values their dignity no less than any other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Today, I want to discuss why passing Intro 131 is not just the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: It is a simple, common sense, and effective policy for solving a widespread under-enforcement problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Intersex people are technically protected by the human rights law due to interpretive enforcement guidance published by the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: However, the absence of an explicit statutory reference to discrimination based on intersex traits has left them vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: For example, even though this interpretation was adopted in 2015, most intersex New Yorkers still have no knowledge that this protection exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: People cannot bring a complaint before the commission to enforce rights they are completely unaware of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: The same is true of those subject to obligation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: under discrimination law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Employers and service providers are not on sufficient notice that discrimination against intersex individuals is prohibited by the guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: This is especially concerning given the current assault on LGBTQIA plus people and their rights across the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Indeed, even the existing guidance is unstable, since it could be changed in an instant by a new commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Through a simple amendment, Intro 131 would rectify this gap in meaningful enforcement and compliance by explicitly prohibiting discrimination on the basis of a person's sex characteristics, including intersex traits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: The change does not create a new liability regime or alter the Commission's enforcement tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: It merely clarifies the law to ensure that intersex New Yorkers are unequivocally protected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: We appreciate the Commission's support for this clarification, and we welcome the Council to follow suit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: This small legislative change will strengthen compliance, make intersex individuals more aware of their rights, and enhance the ability of the Commission to remedy intersex discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: To codify and strengthen protections for this far too often overlooked segment of New Yorkers, we urge the committee to report this bill to the full council for consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cameron Mukherjee
utterances.text: I would also like to pass up copies of my testimony.

chapters.summary: Elizabeth Cooper, a Fordham Law clinic professor, supports Intro 131 and proposes two amendments. She asks the committee to define intersex traits and move the phrase about sex assigned at birth earlier in the definition of gender.
chapters.title: Elizabeth Cooper proposes amendments to Intro 131

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and thank you so much for this opportunity to testify, Councilmember Caban, for your initial interest in sponsoring this bill and in being so supportive of the Fordham Law Clinic all along the way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: It brings all of us great pride, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: And I also want to say that I'm a very grateful constituent of Councilmember Hanif, so very glad to have this opportunity today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: I join my colleagues in their wholehearted support of Intro 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: And on behalf of my colleagues at Interact, who have been just wonderful community partners for the last two years,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: I actually want to raise two straightforward amendments that will ensure that the human rights law thoroughly protects against discrimination based on gender, particularly for people with intersex traits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: I encourage council members to follow along with the handout that we just distributed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: First, as drafted, the bill would prohibit discrimination based on sex characteristics, including intersex traits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: That's how it currently is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: We encourage the committee to define the term intersex traits to do so explicitly as innate

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: variations in an individual's physical sex characteristics, including internal or external anatomy, hormone production, hormone response, or chromosomes that may not reflect typical or binary notions of male or female development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: This is a widely accepted medical definition, and as a term intersects is not yet commonly understood, including it will help prevent any confusion or unnecessary disputes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: Second, we encourage the committee to move the phrase that currently concludes Section 8102's definition of gender, regardless of the sex assigned to that person at birth, to earlier in the definition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: We are concerned that its current placement may be read to apply only to gender identity and expression,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: the part of the definition of gender that immediately precedes this modifier, rather than more broadly to all of the terms under gender.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: Although a narrower interpretation would be counter to the tendency to read civil rights statutes broadly, it would be prudent to avoid any potential misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: Therefore, if adopted, the amended section would read, the term gender includes, regardless of the sex assigned to that person at birth, colon,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: actual or perceived sex, semicolon, sex characteristics, including intersex traits, semicolon, and gender identity and gender expression, including a person's actual or perceived gender or

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: related self-image, appearance, behavior, expression, or other gender-related characteristics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to speak before you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cooper
utterances.text: If you have any questions, happy to hear them.

chapters.summary: Caban thanks the panel and asks for additional examples of discrimination and thoughts on CCHR outreach. Bryony Price describes immigration forms, binary systems, and misinformation about LGBTQIA educators, and urges destigmatizing conversations and protections.
chapters.title: Caban asks panel about discrimination and outreach; Bryony Price responds

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, I just want to echo my gratitude to this panel as well.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I especially enjoyed working with the students of the clinic, and I'm very excited that you will soon be joining the legal community because we need more folks like you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I'm sure that you have learned through this process that the law is politics.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: All the way down.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And, you know, we may have a federal government that is wielding the law in such a way to hurt people, but that also means that we can wield the law to help people.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I think that this is a piece of legislation that does that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I just enjoyed our conversations.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And thank you for...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Explicitly putting on the record the amendments you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm excited to incorporate them.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I know we spoke about them at our last meeting, waiting for exactly this part of the legislative process to have this hearing so that we had the opportunity to go in and make those amendments.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So looking forward to staying in touch and getting those done.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I just want to extend the same question that I

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: mentioned to the last panel, just giving you an extra opportunity to talk about any other instances of

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: types of discrimination that we should be aware of and thinking about and, you know, thoughts on what CCHR should or could be doing in terms of outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: and education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: No pressure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: One thing I'd like to mention, I myself, I've been in the US.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: This is my ninth year in the US, but I'm still pursuing permanent residency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: I was up for a renewal this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: I've just kind of come back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: But I was reminded in this process how...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Difficult about the intersectionality of this kind of legislation and bill and how difficult and binary that system is and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: how without proper guidance and without proper terminology that you end up having to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: lie in certain aspects on certain forms um because you don't want to flag the system for discrepancy especially I myself I'm a public school educator

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: um there's a lot of like misinformation around our community around um LGBTQIA plus educators um and I think uh

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: a more comprehensive conversation and protections for those people is very important because also that's who are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: young people, our children are like looking to for guidance oftentimes before they're even able to have discussions with their families, etc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: And I think that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: It's very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: important that the conversation becomes destigmatized and the protections are there to ensure that that is possible.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks the panel and calls the final panel on Zoom: Shana Knizhnik, Kathleen Collins, Jillian Miano, Joanne Kim, and Kimberly Zieselman.
chapters.title: Hanif calls final public testimony panel on Zoom

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Our final panel is on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Shana Kisnik, Kathleen Collins, Jillian Miano, Joanne Kim, and Kimberly Zieselman.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We will start with Shauna.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Shauna, are you on the Zoom?

chapters.summary: Shana Knizhnik, senior staff attorney at the ACLU and Interact board member, says she is an intersex woman who came out publicly in 2020. She supports Intro 131 and says public education is crucial because most people do not know what intersex means.
chapters.title: Shana Knizhnik testifies for Intro 131 and public education

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Sorry, I guess it wasn't letting me unmute myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Hi, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Thank you so much to Councilmember Caban for introducing this bill to Chair Hanif, my former councilmember, and Chair Nurse, my current councilmember, for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And thank you all for the opportunity to submit my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I'm so sorry that I am not able to be there in person today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: My name is Shauna Knishnik.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I use she, her pronouns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I am a white woman with short dyed blonde hair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I'm wearing glasses and a blue and white striped shirt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I live and work in New York City, where I have lived essentially my entire adult life, having attended Columbia University and then NYU School of Law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And I've been a Brooklyn resident since 2010.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I was previously a public defender in Manhattan for six years at the Legal Aid Society, and I'm now a senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union's LGBTQ and HIV project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And I'm a current member of the board of directors of Interact, as you've learned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: the largest organization in the United States dedicated to the rights of intersex people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I'm also an intersex woman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I came out publicly in an op-ed in Teen Vogue in 2020 at the age of 32 after a lifetime of secrecy, being lied to, and taught to lie about my own body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And today I am speaking in my personal capacity in support of Intro 131 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: The experience of being intersex, as you've heard from my friends today, is different for every intersex person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: But what connects every single story I've ever heard is that our sex traits, which do not fit typical notions or expectations of male or female bodies, are treated by society at large as a problem to be fixed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Or completely ignored rather than as a beautiful facet of natural human diversity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And that treatment leads to almost uniform experiences of shame and secrecy, as you've heard today from so many of my dear friends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Even within the LGBTQIA plus community, the I can often feel like it stands for invisible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: As a result, intersex people can suffer from exclusion, inaccurate assumptions, which leads to concerningly high rates of discrimination, especially in the areas that the NYC Human Rights Law covers, like housing and employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Although many people who are intersex also identify

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: under other letters of the rainbow acronym, the experiences and treatment of intersex people are unique and deserving of their own recognition, celebration, and equal protection under the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Federal protections for LGBTQIA plus Americans have, as we know, been rolled back and attacked at every level by this current federal administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Specific protections for intersex people that were only recently adopted by the previous administration have been included in those rollbacks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And that includes, of course, in the areas of health care as well as employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: In my day job as a civil rights lawyer, I am actively involved in fighting against these attacks and their impact on LGBTQIA Americans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And every action that we see that targets our transgender siblings, including in the areas of health care, identity documents, education, sports, bathroom access, and more, also impacts intersex people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: However, the absence of explicit recognition of intersex people in federal anti-discrimination laws makes protecting our rights much more complicated and difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: The rollbacks and attacks at the federal level, as well as across numerous other jurisdictions at the state and local level, have been ramping up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Your time has expired?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Apologize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I will just say that I'm so

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: grateful that New York City gets the opportunity to lead the nation in recognizing the reality that sex-like gender identity often does not fit a neat binary and that discrimination based on such traits is unlawful, full stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And I hope that this bill is one more small step in many of the history of intersex people asserting our own existence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to support.

chapters.summary: Caban asks Knizhnik for more examples of discrimination and what CCHR education should look like. Knizhnik says proactive public education about intersex people can make a huge difference alongside anti-discrimination protections.
chapters.title: Caban asks Shana Knizhnik about discrimination and CCHR education

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Go for it.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt this panel for a moment just to be able to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's really good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I am going to pose the same question that I've posed to the previous panels to you of just another opportunity to talk about

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: discrimination that we should be aware of and also in terms of the education that CCHR could or should be doing, what potentially is needed on that front.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then as always, thank you, thank you, thank you for all of your work.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: There should be a prompt coming shortly to be unmuted.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We're working on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: They just unmuted me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Did you want to be away?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Somebody else got unmuted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Yeah, Kathy Collins.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Wait, hang on.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We're going to...

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we go to you, Kathy.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: That person's muted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hugh Rose Evans
utterances.text: Hey, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: We love technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the kind words, Tiffany.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I think my colleagues and my friends have spoken so eloquently about their own experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: I will just add, I do think that the public education component is so crucial, and that's something that can really make a huge difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: Obviously, with respect to discrimination protections, we're talking about harms that have already occurred.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: But the ability of the New York City government to be proactive in reaching out to communities, including LGBTQIA plus communities, but also the larger

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: public in understanding what intersex is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: It's such a simple thing, but something that just is not yet even on most folks'radar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shana Knizhnik
utterances.text: And so I would just encourage even broader, you know, the public education component can be a huge aspect, in addition, of course, to the health care pieces that my friends have spoken about as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryony Price
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks Knizhnik and moves to Kathleen Collins on Zoom.
chapters.title: Hanif moves to Kathleen Collins

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We'll now move to Kathleen Collins.

chapters.summary: Kathleen Collins, a congenital quadruple amputee and lawyer, says she shares common experiences with intersex panelists about bodies being seen as needing fixing. She says CCHR must educate city agencies and staff, fix its complaint website, and set enforceable deadlines.
chapters.title: Kathleen Collins testifies on disability rights, CCHR training, and website issues

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: My name is Kathleen Collins.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I'm a Caucasian woman with graying hair, wearing pink headphones, blood background, and wearing a red nose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I'm a congenital quadruple amputee who has lived and was born in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I'd first like to say I found this hearing very interesting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I learned a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And I see a lot of commonality between all our communities in that I, too, deal with people saying about my body and it needing to be fixed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And, you know, you're not beautiful being the way you are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: It took me to the age of like around 58 to be able to say out loud that I am beautiful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And so I hear everything and I really believe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And we have similar, actually we have pretty much the same problems with about access to health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I know many times still today in 2026, we still can't get into dentist's office and doctor's office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And when you go for medical treatment, they say, where's your assistant to help you on to the examining table?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: It's still a problem for all of us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And so discrimination against anyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: is wrong and we need education of everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: The Commission on Human Rights must better educate city agencies, the city council, because they have city council offices that are not accessible to people with disabilities even today,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: businesses and the public that disability rights are civil rights protected by law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Not optional acts of kindness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: That's what we see constantly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Its own staff also need stronger training in disability rights and accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: There are free courses by the federal government on accessibility that I've taken myself and anyone here can take.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: It's called Accessibility Online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: The Commission must have adequate funding, clear accountability, and an effective process for investigating and resolving discrimination complaints promptly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: People with disabilities should not have to wait years for justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Recently, yesterday, I went on to their website to see how you would file a formal complaint on the Commission's website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And apparently there is no way to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: What you have to do, I guess, is reach out to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: What you do is a discrimination report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And then later, I guess, they reach out to you for a formal complaint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And I find that this could cause problems for people because they may think by filing the discrimination report that they're making a legal complaint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Complaint and they may miss filing deadlines and lose their rights, legal rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: So I really think we need to fix that on the website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I'm a lawyer and I understood the nuances and the differences, but I think many lay people may not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Another thing, I looked at the Commission's accessibility reports from 2024, 2025, and 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And if you notice on page four and five of both reports, they just talk about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: putting on repeating about their delays in identifying funding for digital accessibility, effective communications, and workplace inclusion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: They just keep rolling it over at the deadline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: We need fixed deadlines so things can get done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I know Clement So talked about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: If we don't have fixed deadlines, nothing gets done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: So we really need that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Another thing, I thought it was great that we had Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Mosam Meta speak today about Intro 1107-2026 about service animals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: I think that's a good bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: However, I don't have a service animal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: And thus, I urge the council to consult with the leaders in our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Terrence Page, the president of the Greater New York Council of the Blind, which is part of the American Council of the Blind of New York State

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: and National American Council of the Blind, and Rashida Bunting, the first vice president of the National Federation of the Blind of New York State, which is also part of a national organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Thank you, Kathy.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Can you wrap up your final sentence and we'll be reading your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Finally, I just think the council members need to provide the commission with the funding, training, oversight, and enforceable deadlines necessary to deliver results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: Disability rights are civil rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathleen Collins
utterances.text: It's time the commission acted like it.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can you wrap up your final sentence and we'll be reading your testimony.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks Collins and moves to Jillian Miano.
chapters.title: Hanif moves to Jillian Miano

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Jillian Miano.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Jillian Miano, an autistic self-advocate, says landlords rejected her dogs until they became emotional support animals and the process invaded her medical privacy. She supports Intro 1107 and Resolution 665 calling for UNCRPD ratification.
chapters.title: Jillian Miano testifies on service animals, housing privacy, and UNCRPD

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and members of the Committee on Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: My name is Jillian.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: I am a resident of New York City, testifying regarding Intro 1107-2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: I am an advocate for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities, as well as a 28-year-old woman on the autism spectrum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: As an individual who has moved time and time again with my family, I have faced many landlords rejecting my dogs because they felt they would be a nuisance to neighbors or just wouldn't accept them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: There was a time I had nowhere to go due to a mold-infested home I was living in for six years with my family,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: and when I had no choice but to stay with other family members, and the landlords that rejected us would say, and I quote, We will only take your dogs if they are emotional support animals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: I do not want to leave my dogs in the cold or give them away because I...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: Created a bond with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: I had no choice but to make my dogs emotional support animals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: The interview process and paperwork was very personal, which I understand to a certain degree, but to ask for what medications I am on and other aspects that I felt were very private is absurd.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: I feel that there should be a different way to have an emotional support animal or service dog.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: There should be questions that are not as deep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: that this department goes into his questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: While Intro 1107-2026 focuses on educating business owners about where emotional support animals cannot go, the council must also address the city handles

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: the privacy rights of who needs these animals, public campaigns,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: must make it clear that a person's dignity and medical privacy should not be compromised just to receive a housing accommodation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: And also, I would like to speak today on Resolution 0665-2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: I want our country to ratify the UN Convention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: On the rights of persons with disabilities, this treaty focuses on human rights acceptance and making sure society removes barriers for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: Passing this resolution shows that New York City stands up for the rights of people with disabilities, neurodivergent like me, and millions of other people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: I feel the rights of individuals with disabilities has gone unnoticed in many ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: Please vote yes to this resolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jillian Miano
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Council staff thanks Miano and moves to Joanne Kim.
chapters.title: Staff moves to Joanne Kim

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We'll now move on to Joanne Kim.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Joanne Kim, assistant director at the Korean American Family Service Center, supports Intro 131. She says immigrant survivors of gender-based violence face compounded barriers and no one should have to choose between living authentically and living safely.
chapters.title: Joanne Kim supports Intro 131 for immigrant survivors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: My name is Joanne Kim, and I'm an Assistant Director of Community Engagement at the Korean American Family Service Center, KAFSC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: For nearly four decades, KAFSC has supported immigrant survivors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: of domestic violence, sexual assault, and other forms of gender-based violence through culturally responsive, trauma-informed services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: On behalf of KFSC, I am here today in support of Intro 0131-2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: At KFSC, our work is rooted in a feminist understanding that gender-based violence is not simply an individual experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: It is connected to broader systems of inequality, discrimination, and control over people's bodies, identities, and choices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: For immigrant survivors, these inequalities are often compounded by language barriers, cultural stigma, financial dependence, and fear of navigating unfamiliar institutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Consider an immigrant survivor who has experienced abuse and is seeking

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: They may already fear speaking out because of their immigrant status, limited English proficiency, or dependence on their abuser.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: If that individual also faces discrimination because of their sex characteristics or intersex traits,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Another barrier is placed between them and the protection that they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: While this is an illustrative example, the barriers are ones we encounter every day in our work with immigrant survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: No one should have to choose between living authentically and living safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Intro 131 is important because it is explicitly recognized as sex characteristics, including intersex traits, within the definition of gender under the city's human rights law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: From a feminist perspective, this is about bodily autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: dignity, and the fundamental right of every person to exist without discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: At KFSC, we believe that ending gender-based violence requires us to challenge the systems that make people vulnerable to abuse and exclusion in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: We urge the City Council to advance Intro 131 and ensure that these protections are understood and accessible to immigrant communities, including

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: those with limited English proficiency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Kim
utterances.text: Because safety, dignity, and freedom from discrimination should never depend on who you are, how you identify,

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Or where you come from.

chapters.summary: Council staff thanks Kim and moves to Kimberly Zieselman.
chapters.title: Staff moves to Kimberly Zieselman

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We'll now move on to Kimberly Zieselman.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Kimberly Zieselman, senior advisor at Outright International, says she learned she was intersex at age 40. She says explicit statutory protection in New York City would provide clarity and visibility and could have global impact.
chapters.title: Kimberly Zieselman supports Intro 131 and global intersex rights

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: Hi, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: My name is Kimberly Zieselman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: I am an intersex woman, an attorney, a human rights defender, and the senior advisor for global intersex rights at Outright International, which is a global LGBTIQ human rights organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: I also previously served as executive director of Interact Advocates for Intersex Youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: I'm here today speaking both professionally on behalf of Outright and personally as an intersex person in support of Intro 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: Like many intersex people, I grew up not knowing the truth about my own body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: In fact, I didn't learn I was intersex or what was done to me as a child until I was 40 years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: That experience taught me firsthand the profound consequences of intersex invisibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: Today, I work with intersex human rights defenders around the globe, many of whom are fighting simply to have their existence acknowledged and their basic rights protected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: Outright has documented cases around the world in which intersex people have been rejected by their families, expelled from schools, harassed at work, and subjected to physical and sexual violence simply due

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: to bias based on their perceived differences, their sex characteristics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: And yet here in the United States, intersex people remain largely invisible in our civil rights laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: New York City has already recognized that discrimination against intersex people as prohibited under its human rights law, but those protections are not explicitly written into the statute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: And the rights that people don't know they have are rights that they may never exercise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: So this bill would change that by explicitly protecting people from discrimination based on sex characteristics, including intersex traits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: And New York City would provide greater clarity, visibility, and recognition to our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: According to Interact, this would be the first explicit statutory civil rights protection of its kind in the United States.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: And for intersex New Yorkers, that really matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: And for intersex advocates around the world and community members, it also matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: As we know, for better or for worse, what happens here in the United States often has a big impact globally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: We cannot protect people fully if we don't even name them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: So on behalf of Outright International, I respectfully urge the Council to advance Introduction 131.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Zieselman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks Zieselman and calls Sayer Russell, who is present in the room.
chapters.title: Hanif calls Sayer Russell

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Sayer Russell, who is here with us.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And you may begin whenever you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sayer Russell, founder of Autistic Adults NYC, supports recognizing June 18 as Autistic Pride Day. He says representation and understanding shape how autistic people see themselves and urges the city to involve autistic people in decisions about services and messaging.
chapters.title: Sayer Russell supports Autistic Pride Day and autistic representation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: My name is Sayer Russell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: For folks who need a visual description, I'm a black, Hispanic, trans, masculine person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: I've got short curly hair, wearing a blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: I live in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: I'm an autistic person, and I'm the founder of Autistic Adults NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: We're an autistic-run nonprofit, and we serve the autistic community here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: I'm here today in support of recognizing June 18th as Autistic Pride Day in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Thank you, the council, for hearing this resolution to everyone who supported it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: The past four years, my nonprofit has held annual Autistic Pride Day celebrations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: It's something that's meaningful to many of our community members, but also very meaningful to me personally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: When I was growing up, my family and I knew I was different, but I wasn't formally recognized as autistic until I was in graduate school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: And I think about how different things might have been if I'd grown up with a better understanding of autism, seen more positive representations of autistic people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Or autistic people who look like myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Instead, I had a very limited deficit-based understanding of what autism meant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: And that experience has shown me how much representation and understanding can shape how we see ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Autistic Pride Day encourages autistic people to be open and vocal about our lives, sharing our unique experiences without being made to feel ashamed of who we are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: It pushes back against messages that portray autism as a tragedy, something to fear, or something that needs to be fixed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: And importantly, it was a day started by autistic people for autistic people and centers autistic voices and gives us the opportunity to speak for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Not only is that important for representation, but it's also important for our communities and for the city's role in shaping autistic lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Autistic people face barriers in almost all aspects of our lives, from education to health care to employment to housing to accessing supports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Too often, decisions are made without our input, leading to systems that misunderstand our needs or fail to provide meaningful support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: We cannot address these barriers without listening to the people that experience them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: So I hope Autistic Pride Day is recognized in New York City as a day for autistic people to be visible and not just talked about, and as an opportunity to promote positive representation rather than negativity around autism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: And I also hope the city embraces the spirit of Autistic Pride Day by involving autistic people in decisions about our community, including services for autistic people, training about autistic people, and public messaging campaigns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Without autistic input, messages can often be infantilizing, focus exclusively on deficits, or rely on outdated symbols that don't reflect our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Recognizing this day is an opportunity for New York City to acknowledge autistic people's experiences, celebrate our contributions, and take our perspective seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: And I hope it helps move us towards a city where autistic people are not just talked about, but heard and understood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sayer Russell
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks Russell and moves back to Zoom for Edward Funches.
chapters.title: Hanif moves to Edward Funches on Zoom

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We're going to go back to the Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Edward Funches.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Edward Funches says the disability community has the highest unemployment rate and that this contributes to housing instability. He describes creating Inclusion to provide jobs for people with disabilities, formerly incarcerated people, and others, and calls for more partnerships with city agencies.
chapters.title: Edward Funches testifies on unemployment, housing, and Inclusion company

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: Hello, I want to thank you all for allowing me and us to have this opportunity to speak with y'all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I want to speak about unemployment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: The disability community has the highest unemployment rate in any community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: And this is why we have individuals in bad situations of housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I came home from doing some time, and I was told I couldn't go back to any housing because of the charges that I had, which was drug charges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I was fortunate enough to get some assistance from the late Charlie Rangel, which helped me out a great deal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: So I created the company 12 years ago called Inclusion,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: provide job opportunities for the disadvantaged community, people with disabilities, formerly incarcerated individuals, people experiencing homelessness, and veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: And I think if we start right there, helping individuals out, the problem, another one of the problems that we have is people are in those positions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I want to tell you about...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: A former deputy mayor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I happened to see him in front of City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: He said on his statements, he had, when the city becomes fairer and more inclusive, we all benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I believe that then and I believe it now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: However, he didn't believe that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I seen him in front of City Hall and I approached him to tell him how much I appreciated those words.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: Before I could say anything else, he said to me, I don't have any change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: And this is the problem that we have right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: People in those positions are not really giving us the assistance that we need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: So I'm thankful that we're having this meeting right here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: And we need to have more of these meetings and put people in positions that can help individuals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: I created this company and we've been doing extremely well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: But we need to partner with agencies or with city elected officials that believe in making a change for these communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Funches
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks everyone who testified and asks if anyone else wishes to speak. She notes written testimony can be submitted within 72 hours and closes the hearing, thanking attendees and looking forward to passing the bills.
chapters.title: Hanif thanks witnesses, notes written testimony, and closes hearing

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to everyone who has testified.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If there's anyone present in the room or on Zoom that hasn't had the opportunity to testify, please raise your hand.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Seeing no one else, I would like to note that written testimony, which will be reviewed in full by committee staff, may be submitted to the record up to 72 hours after the close of this hearing by emailing it to testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all so much, and especially to those who are here in 250 Broadway, our chambers.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you for sticking around.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This was a very, very informative hearing on so many fronts.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Really appreciate everyone's work, advocacy, and I look forward to getting the bills that were heard today passed.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all.

summary: Committee on Disabilities joint with Civil and Human Rights held an oversight hearing on CCHR disability enforcement trends and four bills/resolutions.
CCHR and MOPD testified on disability discrimination complaints, Project Equal Access, staffing, case timelines, and coordination.
Public testimony covered service animal access, intersex protections, Autistic Pride Day, shelter and housing discrimination, and UNCRPD ratification.
title: Committee on Disabilities
topic: Oversight topic - Commission on Human Rights Disability Enforcement Trends
